0.title: Romans
0.overview:
Martin Luther called the letter to the Romans "the chief part of the New Testament and the very purest gospel." John Calvin wrote that "when anyone understands this Epistle, he has a passage opened to him to the understanding of the whole Scripture." Martyn Lloyd-Jones preached 366 sermons on it over some thirteen years and still felt he had not exhausted it. Romans is not one letter among many; it is the theological heart of the New Testament, the fullest and most systematic exposition of the gospel that God ever moved a human pen to write.

Paul wrote to a church he had never visited, in the capital of the empire, at the height of his apostolic ministry — probably from Corinth around AD 57. His purpose was not merely to introduce himself before a planned visit to Spain. It was to set before these believers, Jew and Gentile alike, the full panorama of the gospel: the universal guilt of humanity, the righteousness of God revealed in Christ, justification by faith alone, the transforming work of the Spirit, the sovereign purposes of God in election and in the mystery of Israel, and the shape of the redeemed life in the world. No letter covers more ground. No letter has changed more lives.

The structure follows the gospel's own logic. Chapters 1–3 establish the diagnosis: all humanity — pagan, moralist, and Jew — stands guilty before the righteous God, with no resources of its own to secure acquittal. Chapters 3–5 announce the remedy: the righteousness of God given freely through faith in Jesus Christ, who bore the wrath we deserved. Chapters 6–8 trace the fruit: union with Christ, death to sin, life in the Spirit, adoption as children, and the unshakeable security of those whom God has called. Chapters 9–11 address the mystery: if Israel is the covenant people, why has Israel largely rejected its Messiah? And chapters 12–16 show what the gospel-transformed life looks like in home, church, city, and empire.

Who were the Christians in Rome? No apostle founded the church. Luke lists visitors from Rome in the Pentecost crowd (Acts 2:10), and the gospel probably reached the capital through Jewish believers like them. Some years before this letter Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2), and for a time the congregations were largely Gentile. When Jewish believers returned after his death, they came back to churches whose leaders and habits had changed. That tension between Jewish and Gentile Christians lies behind much of the letter, especially chapters 9–11 and 14–15 (cf. 1:7).

And what of the New Perspective on Paul? Since the 1970s scholars such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright have argued that first-century Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation; that works of the law means chiefly the marks that set Jews apart, such as circumcision, the food laws and the Sabbath; and that justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people. They are right that the unity of Jew and Gentile is a real concern of Romans (3:29–30; 15:7), and that Judaism has sometimes been described unfairly. But the more likely reading is the Reformation one. Paul’s charge in 1:18–3:20 is not that Jews kept Gentiles out but that all have broken God’s law and stand guilty before him, so that every mouth may be stopped (3:19). Justification answers that guilt. It is God’s verdict of acquittal, given freely to the ungodly (4:5) on the ground of Christ’s blood (5:9). Belonging to God’s people follows from that verdict; it is not what the verdict means.

We will draw on the great Reformed interpreters of this letter: Calvin's magisterial commentary, Luther whose reading of 1:17 unlocked the Reformation, Lloyd-Jones whose fourteen volumes remain the richest English-language treatment, John Stott whose Message of Romans is a model of accessible depth, Timothy Keller's Romans for You, and scholars Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner. Come expecting to be undone and remade. Romans has that effect on everyone who takes it seriously.

1.title: The Gospel and the Wrath of God
1.overview:
Romans 1 opens with one of the most carefully crafted sentences in ancient literature — a single Greek sentence spanning seven verses, in which Paul introduces himself, his gospel, and his Lord with the precision of a theologian and the ardour of a man in love with what he believes. By the time the chapter ends, the same pen that wrote of the gospel as "the power of God for salvation" has traced the terrifying arc of divine wrath against human idolatry. These two things belong together: the good news is only truly good when the bad news is truly bad.

The movement of the chapter is deliberate. Paul establishes the gospel (vv. 1–17), then demonstrates the need for it (vv. 18–32). The power of God for salvation is proportionate to the depth of human lostness — and that depth, as Paul will show, is vertiginous. The world Paul describes in vv. 18–32 is not ancient history; it is every human culture that has suppressed the knowledge of the God it cannot stop knowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Paul, the Gospel, and the Grace of Apostleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's opening sentence is a controlled explosion of theology. In seven verses he identifies himself as a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God — a gospel promised in the Old Testament Scriptures, concerning God's Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and declared to be the Son of God in power by the resurrection from the dead. Every phrase is a chapter of theology waiting to be unfolded. This is not a man warming up; this is a man who knows exactly what he believes and why it matters.

The word that unlocks everything is euangelion — gospel. It meant, in the first-century Roman world, the proclamation of good news, typically the accession of a new emperor or a great military victory. Paul seizes the word and repurposes it entirely. The great news is not that Caesar has triumphed; it is that Jesus Christ, Son of God, Lord, has been raised from the dead and now reigns over all things. This is a message with empire-shaking implications — which is precisely why Paul is eager to preach it in Rome itself.

The address of grace and peace — "to all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints" — is not a formality. It is a theological declaration. These people, in the capital of pagan power, are loved by God. They are called. They are saints — not by virtue of their moral achievement but by virtue of their union with Jesus Christ who is holy, and who has made them holy in him. Before Paul preaches a word of gospel to them, he speaks a word of gospel over them. This is the Pauline method: ground identity before applying imperatives.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pre-Pauline Gospel

One of the most important features of Romans 1:1–4 is Paul's insistence that the gospel he preaches was "promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures." The gospel is not a Pauline invention or a Gentile innovation — it is the fulfilment of Israel's own scriptures. Jesus is the descendant of David (2 Samuel 7), declared Son of God by resurrection (Psalm 2). Calvin saw in this the unity of the two testaments: the Old Testament is the gospel in promise; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment. Any reading of the Old Testament that does not find Christ there has missed its point.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's designation of himself as a doulos — slave — of Christ Jesus was shocking in a world where slavery was degradation. He inverts the social order: the highest dignity available to a human being is not freedom but bondage to Jesus Christ. Now: In an age that prizes autonomy above all things, the Christian claim that the best possible life is one of radical submission to Christ still provokes the same offence — and still offers the same liberation to those who discover that the lordship of Christ is the only yoke that is easy and the only burden that is light.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul introduces himself by three things that define him: Christ’s slave, called as an apostle, set apart for God’s gospel.

Servant. Doulos, slave: wholly owned by Christ.

Called. By God’s initiative (Galatians 1:15).

Set apart. Perhaps a play on “Pharisee” (separated one): now separated for the gospel.

The gospel of God. God’s good news, not Paul’s invention.

Romans. Written from Corinth about AD 57, to a church Paul had not founded, preparing for a mission to Spain (15:24). The fullest statement of the gospel in Scripture.
verseByVerse.note: “Servant” translates the ordinary word for a slave, one wholly owned by his master. Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably around AD 57, before taking the collection to Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel is not new: God promised it in the Scriptures, and it is about his Son, born of David’s line.

Promised beforehand. The gospel fulfils the Old Testament (Luke 24:27).

Concerning his Son. The gospel is about a person.

Descended from David. His true humanity and messianic right.

parallels.desc: the promised son of David

verseByVerse.quote: and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,
verseByVerse.commentary:
By his resurrection, Jesus was installed as the Son of God in power.

Declared. Appointed, installed, not made Son: he already was (v. 3). Where Christians differ. Adoptionists read this as Jesus becoming God’s Son at the resurrection. Paul says the gospel is “concerning his Son” who then came in the flesh. Verdict: the eternal Son, who became man, was enthroned in power as the risen Messiah.

According to the Spirit of holiness. The Holy Spirit, or the new era of the Spirit, in contrast with “according to the flesh”.

Jesus Christ our Lord. His full title.

parallels.desc: you are my Son

verseByVerse.quote: ...through whom we have received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations, including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ... — Romans 1:5-6
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Christ Paul received grace and apostleship to bring the nations to the obedience that comes from faith.

The obedience of faith. Obedience that springs from faith, or the obedience that consists in believing. Both: faith submits to God (16:26).

For the sake of his name. Mission aims at Christ’s glory.

Including you. The Roman Christians are among the called nations.

parallels.desc: the obedience of faith

verseByVerse.quote: To all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. — Romans 1:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church in Rome is loved by God, called to be holy, and greeted with grace and peace.

Loved and called. Identity before duty.

Textual note. A few manuscripts omit “in Rome” here and in verse 15, perhaps so that the letter could be read generally. Verdict: original.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people — all believers. The church at Rome was not founded by Paul; he had never been there.

parallels.desc: visitors from Rome at Pentecost

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Paul's Longing and His Debt to All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established his gospel and his greeting, Paul opens his heart. He has prayed for the Roman Christians unceasingly. He has longed to visit them. He has been prevented — more than once. This passage is often passed over quickly on the way to the theological fireworks of vv. 16–17, but it deserves careful attention: it shows us what a gospel-shaped pastor looks like. Paul's longing is not merely strategic (Rome as a missionary base) but personal. He wants to see them, to be mutually encouraged, to share with them some spiritual gift.

The phrase "I am under obligation" (v. 14) — literally "I am a debtor" — is startling. Paul does not feel that preaching the gospel to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish, is above and beyond the call of duty. He feels indebted to them. They have a claim on him. The grace that was lavished on him on the Damascus road was not for his private enrichment; it was for their benefit. He owes them what he received for free. This is the logic of all gospel ministry: grace received creates obligation discharged.

"I am not ashamed of the gospel" (v. 16) — the understatement implies the opposite: he is eagerly proud of it, itching to proclaim it in Rome's very centre. Rome was the most intimidating platform imaginable: the seat of empire, the crossroads of civilization, the city that had crucified the Lord of the gospel. And Paul cannot wait to get there.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pastoral and Missionary Logic of Paul

Romans 1:8–15 reveals that Paul's missionary strategy is inseparable from his pastoral affection. He does not view the Roman church as an audience for his theology or a resource for his mission; he views them as beloved brothers and sisters in whom he longs to rejoice. Reformed missiology has always insisted that mission and church are inseparable — the mission proceeds from the church, through the church, and for the establishment of the church. Paul's eagerness to visit Rome exemplifies this: he is not a lone-ranger evangelist but an apostle embedded in the body of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's sense of debt to all people — Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish — erased every cultural and social hierarchy. The gospel belonged to no class or culture. Now: The contemporary church is perpetually tempted to preach a gospel shaped for those who are already culturally similar to us. Paul's "debtor" language is a rebuke: the gospel is owed to every person in our reach, regardless of whether they seem like likely converts or comfortable neighbours.

verseByVerse.quote: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I mention you
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God that the Roman church’s faith is known everywhere, and he prays for them constantly.

Through Jesus Christ. Even thanksgiving comes through Christ.

The whole world. News travelled to and from the capital.

In my spirit. Wholehearted service.

verseByVerse.quote: always in my prayers, asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that God will at last allow him to visit them.

By God’s will. Paul plans, but submits his plans to God (James 4:15). He did come, in chains (Acts 28).

verseByVerse.quote: For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you — that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith, both yours and mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul longs to strengthen them, and to be strengthened by them: ministry flows both ways.

Some spiritual gift. Probably not a charismatic gift but a spiritual blessing, encouragement and teaching.

Mutually encouraged. The apostle expects to receive as well as give.

On a Tuesday. Go to church expecting both to give and to receive.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented), in order that I may reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has often planned to come and been prevented; he wants a harvest among them as among other Gentiles.

Prevented. By his work elsewhere (15:22).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “brothers” can include sisters in the church.

verseByVerse.quote: I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome. — Romans 1:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul owes the gospel to everyone, so he is eager to preach it in Rome.

Under obligation. A debtor: the gospel entrusted to him is owed to all.

Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish. Every culture and class.

On a Tuesday. You owe the gospel to your neighbours. How will you pay the debt?
verseByVerse.note: Greeks thought of all non-Greek speakers as “barbarians.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — The Theme: The Righteousness of God by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two verses. The entire letter in miniature. Everything Paul will argue across sixteen chapters is compressed here with the density of a diamond. "I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written: 'The righteous shall live by faith.'" This is the thesis statement of Romans, and it is the sentence that changed the world.

Martin Luther, tormented by the phrase "the righteousness of God" — understanding it as the terrifying standard by which God condemns sinners — wrestled with it until the light broke. "At last," he wrote, "meditating day and night...I began to understand that the righteousness of God is that by which the righteous lives by a gift of God, namely by faith. And this is the meaning: the righteousness of God is revealed by the gospel, namely, the passive righteousness with which the merciful God justifies us by faith. Here I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates." The Reformation began in these two verses.

The gospel is power — not advice, not inspiration, not a moral framework, but the very power of God actively at work to save. It is power for salvation — not merely forgiveness of past sins, but the complete rescue of a human being from the dominion of sin and death and the wrath of God, and the restoration of that person to the full flourishing of life in God. And it is for everyone who believes — the one condition, the one instrument, the one hand that receives what God freely gives: faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Righteousness of God: Attribute or Gift?

Reformed exegesis has understood "the righteousness of God" in Romans 1:17 as a righteousness that originates with God and is given by God to the believing sinner — what the Reformers called iustitia aliena, an alien righteousness, a righteousness that is not our own. Luther's breakthrough was recognising that this righteousness is not the demanding standard that condemns but the gracious gift that saves. This is the doctrine of imputation: Christ's perfect righteousness is credited to the account of the believing sinner, so that God can be simultaneously just (the sin has been punished in Christ) and the justifier (the sinner is declared righteous). Calvin called this the "wonderful exchange" — Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luther's discovery of Romans 1:17 broke the back of a system of salvation by merit and religious performance that had enslaved Western Christendom for centuries. The Reformation was, at its heart, a rediscovery of these two verses. Now: Every generation re-erects the system of merit that the gospel demolishes. Every human heart, left to itself, believes it must earn its standing with God. Romans 1:16–17 is the permanent, repeatable antidote: the gospel is not something you do; it is something done for you, received by faith, given by the merciful God who justifies the ungodly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. — Romans 1:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is not ashamed of the gospel, because it is God’s own power to save everyone who believes.

Not ashamed. In Rome, capital of power, a crucified Messiah looked foolish (1 Corinthians 1:23).

The power of God. The gospel does not merely describe salvation; it brings it (1 Corinthians 1:18).

Everyone who believes. The only condition is faith.

To the Jew first. A priority in history and in mission (Acts 13:46).

verseByVerse.quote: For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith.' — Romans 1:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the gospel God reveals a righteousness that comes from him, received by faith from first to last, as Habakkuk said.

The righteousness of God. Where Christians differ. Medieval theology often read this as God’s justice that punishes; Luther discovered it as the righteousness God gives to sinners by faith. The New Perspective emphasises God’s covenant faithfulness. Verdict: the gift of a righteous status from God (3:21–22; Philippians 3:9), which also displays his own righteousness and faithfulness (3:26).

From faith for faith. By faith from start to finish.

Habakkuk 2:4. The righteous shall live by faith: the theme verse of the letter.

For worship. Thank God for a righteousness you could never earn.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “from faith for faith” can also be rendered “beginning and ending in faith,” and the quotation “The one who by faith is righteous shall live.”

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–32 — The Wrath of God and the Ruin of Idolatry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having announced the gospel, Paul immediately establishes why it is necessary. The gospel is good news only against the backdrop of very bad news — and the bad news Paul now delivers is as stark and unsparing as anything in Scripture. God's wrath is being revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who suppress the truth in unrighteousness. The problem is not ignorance; it is suppression. Humanity knows God — knows him through creation, through conscience — and actively holds that knowledge down, refusing its implications, fleeing from its demands.

The structure of vv. 18–32 is a three-stage description of idolatry's logic and its consequences. First, the knowledge of God is suppressed (vv. 18–20). Then, God is exchanged for idols — images of creatures replacing the uncreated Creator (vv. 21–23). Then, God gives them up — three times that terrible phrase appears (vv. 24, 26, 28) — abandoning them to the sexual and moral dissolution that is both the consequence and the judgment of their idolatry. The wrath of God is not primarily a future event; it is a present reality, operating through the structure of a moral universe that reaps what it sows.

This passage is not a description of the worst of humanity — the serial killers and tyrants. It is a description of normal human culture operating without the restraining grace of God. The Rome to which Paul wrote would have recognised itself in these verses. So would every culture in every age. So would every human heart that is honest enough to look clearly at itself.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Wrath of God

Reformed theology has insisted, against every attempt to soften or allegorize it, that the wrath of God is real, personal, and active. It is not merely the impersonal outworking of a moral law (as C.H. Dodd argued), nor a primitive metaphor for natural consequences. It is the holy, settled, righteous opposition of the living God to everything that contradicts his character. Leon Morris showed definitively that in both Testaments, divine wrath is personal and purposeful — God's moral revulsion at sin, expressed in active judgment. The gospel is only fully good news when this wrath is fully real: Christ bore the wrath we deserved (3:25), and those who are in Christ are saved from the wrath to come (5:9).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's description of idol worship in vv. 22–23 — exchanging the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal creatures — described the Roman religious world exactly. The pantheon of Rome was populated by humanised gods and deified emperors, all of them creatures rather than Creator. Now: The idols have changed shape but not substance. We exchange the glory of God for the image of the successful career, the perfect family, the autonomous self, the entertained mind. Every idol is a creature thing promoted to Creator status — and Paul's analysis of the consequences (futile thinking, darkened hearts, moral dissolution) maps precisely onto what happens when any created thing is made to bear the weight only God can carry.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel is needed because God’s wrath is already being revealed against all human godlessness and wickedness that suppresses the truth.

Wrath. God’s settled, holy opposition to evil.

Is revealed. Present tense: seen now in God giving people over to their sins (vv. 24, 26, 28), and finally on the day of wrath (2:5).

Suppress the truth. The root problem is not ignorance but resistance.

verseByVerse.quote: For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has made himself known through creation, so that no one is without excuse.

Plain to them. General revelation: creation reveals God’s eternal power and divine nature (Psalm 19:1–4).

Without excuse. Enough light to condemn, not enough to save.

Where Christians differ: natural theology. Some (Aquinas) build a positive case for God from reason; others (Karl Barth) reject natural theology altogether. Reformed theology holds that creation truly reveals God, but sinners suppress it, so only Scripture and the Spirit bring saving knowledge (Westminster Confession 1.1). Verdict: creation speaks clearly; the fault lies with the hearer.

parallels.desc: the heavens declare the glory of God

verseByVerse.quote: For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing God, humanity refused to honour him or thank him, and its thinking became futile.

Did not honour or thank. Ingratitude is the root of rebellion.

Futile. Empty reasoning.

Claiming to be wise. Intellectual pride led to folly.

On a Tuesday. Thankfulness is not optional; it is the first mark of knowing God.

parallels.desc: they went after worthlessness

verseByVerse.quote: and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Humanity traded the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal creatures.

Exchanged. A key word (vv. 23, 25, 26): sin is a bad trade.

Images. Psalm 106:20; Jeremiah 2:11. Idolatry includes anything that takes God’s place.

parallels.desc: they exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s judgment is to hand people over to the desires they have chosen, so that idolatry leads to degradation.

God gave them up. Three times (vv. 24, 26, 28). Judgment begins as God lets people have what they want.

The lie. That the creature is worthy of worship.

Blessed for ever. Paul cannot mention the Creator without praising him.
verseByVerse.note: “Gave them up” means God handed them over to what they chose — his judgment working through their own desires.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature; and the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another, men committing shameless acts with men and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turning from the Creator leads to turning from the created design for sexuality.

Contrary to nature. Against the created order of male and female (Genesis 1:27; 2:24).

Where Christians differ. Some modern interpreters argue Paul condemns only exploitative relationships, not committed same-sex unions. The language of creation and nature, and the consistent witness of Scripture, point to all same-sex sexual practice. Verdict: the historic Christian view: same-sex sexual practice is contrary to God’s design. It is stated with care: Paul’s point is that all humanity has turned from God (3:23); same-sex attraction is not itself the sin, and people who experience it must be loved, welcomed and offered the same gospel and the same call to holiness as all of us.

Receiving the due penalty. Sin carries its own consequences.

verseByVerse.quote: And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refusing to acknowledge God leads to a mind that can no longer judge rightly.

Did not see fit. A wordplay: they did not approve God, so God gave them an unapproved mind.

A debased mind. Moral reasoning itself is corrupted.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay: because they did not “see fit” (edokimasan) to acknowledge God, he gave them up to a “debased” (adokimon, literally “unfit”) mind.

verseByVerse.quote: They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. They are gossips,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The result is every kind of wrongdoing, especially sins against others.

A vice list. Most of these are ordinary, respectable sins: greed, envy, malice, deceit, gossip.

verseByVerse.quote: slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list continues: slander, hatred of God, arrogance, disobedience to parents, faithlessness, heartlessness and ruthlessness.

Disobedient to parents. Placed alongside the gravest sins.

On a Tuesday. Find yourself in the list before you point to others (2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Though they know God's righteous decree that those who practice such things deserve to die, they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing that such things deserve death, people not only do them but applaud others who do.

Know God’s decree. Conscience testifies (2:15).

Give approval. The final stage: celebrating sin.

The point of the chapter. All the world is guilty; but Paul is about to turn to the moralist (2:1), and then to the gospel (3:21).

not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented), in order that I may reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles.<sup>14</sup>I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish.<sup>15</sup>So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome.<sup>16</sup>For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.<sup>17</sup>For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, “The righteous shall live by faith.”<sup>18</sup>For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.<sup>19</sup>For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them.<sup>20</sup>For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse.<sup>21</sup>For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened.<sup>22</sup>Claiming to be wise, they became fools,<sup>23</sup>and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things.<sup>24</sup>Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves,<sup>25</sup>because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.<sup>26</sup>For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature;<sup>27</sup>and the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another, men committing shameless acts with men and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.<sup>28</sup>And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done.<sup>29</sup>They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. They are gossips,<sup>30</sup>slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents,<sup>31</sup>foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless.<sup>32</sup>Though they know God’s righteous decree that those who practice such things deserve to die, they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them.

2.title: God's Impartial Judgment
2.overview:
Chapter 1 ended with a catalogue of Gentile vice that a first-century Jewish reader would have heard with satisfaction, nodding along at the depravity of the pagan world. Chapter 2 turns without warning on that same reader: "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges." The trap is sprung. The person who condemns the sins of others while practising the same things is not morally superior to the Gentile; he is, Paul argues, in an even more culpable position — because he knows better.

Paul's target in chapter 2 is not the pagan but the moralist — specifically, the Jewish moralist who believes that covenant membership and religious privilege provide a buffer against divine judgment. They do not. God's judgment is impartial: He renders to each according to his works, to Jew and Gentile alike. The Gentile who has only the law of conscience will be judged by that; the Jew who has the law of Moses will be judged by that. In either case, the verdict will be the same: all fall short.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — God's Righteous and Impartial Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rhetorical brilliance of Romans 2:1 is breathtaking. Paul has spent fifteen verses describing the moral ruin of the Gentile world — and now he wheels on the approving reader: "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things." The knife Paul had been pointing at the Gentile he now turns on anyone who imagines that moral judgment of others places them above judgment themselves.

The principle Paul establishes is foundational: God's judgment is according to truth (v. 2), according to works (v. 6), without partiality (v. 11). These three principles together demolish every form of religious self-satisfaction. "According to truth" means God sees through performance to reality. "According to works" means the whole life is the evidence, not merely the religious moments. "Without partiality" means no ethnic or covenant privilege exempts anyone from accountability before the Judge of all the earth.

Verses 14–15 introduce the remarkable teaching about the conscience as a moral witness — Gentiles who do not have the Torah nonetheless "show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness." This is Paul's doctrine of moral general revelation: human beings are not morally blank. The conscience, however distorted by sin, retains something of the moral law written at creation. This is why all human beings, without exception, will have no excuse on the day of judgment.

Two things in this section deserve naming here, because they are easily lost between the principles. The first is verse 4, the warmest sentence in the passage and the most often misread: the riches of God’s kindness and forbearance and patience are not evidence that he does not mind. They are “meant to lead you to repentance”. Every day on which judgment does not fall is not indifference; it is an invitation still being held open — and Paul’s charge is that we presume on it, reading the delay as a verdict already returned in our favour. The second is verse 16, which tells us when this happens and who conducts it: “on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus”. The Judge is not a principle but a person with a face, and the material to be weighed is not the record other people can see but the secrets. Which is the most frightening sentence in the chapter, or the most freeing — since for those who are his, the one who will weigh what nobody else knows about them is the one who died for it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment According to Works

Romans 2:6–11 appears to teach salvation by works — "to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life." Reformed exegesis has understood this as describing the principle of judgment (God will judge the whole life) rather than the means of salvation (which is faith alone). The person who truly seeks God from the heart will be given — by grace — the faith that produces the works that evidence genuine conversion. Works are the evidence of salvation, never its ground. Paul is not contradicting 1:16–17; he is establishing the standard of divine judgment that makes grace necessary for everyone.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish confidence in covenant privilege — circumcision, Torah, temple — as a buffer against divine judgment was a live pastoral issue in Paul's day. Many Jews believed that while Gentiles might face judgment, the covenant people were secure by virtue of their membership. Paul demolishes this with surgical precision. Now: The equivalent today is the nominal Christian who trusts in baptism, church membership, or moral respectability as a substitute for genuine faith and repentance. Paul's word is the same: God is not impressed by religious credentials. He is looking for the transformed heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things. We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The moral person who condemns others’ sins condemns himself, because he does the same things.

O man. Paul turns to the reader who has been nodding along with chapter 1: the moral Gentile, and especially the Jew (v. 17).

You do the same. Perhaps not every sin, but the same kind: pride, envy, greed, slander (1:29–31).

According to truth. God judges by the facts, not by appearances or excuses.

On a Tuesday. The sin you criticise most in others is often worth checking in yourself (Matthew 7:1–5).

verseByVerse.quote: Do you suppose, O man — you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself — that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not mistake God’s patience for approval; his kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.

Presume. Treat lightly, take for granted.

Kindness, forbearance, patience. God’s delay is mercy (2 Peter 3:9).

Leads to repentance. Not fear only, but kindness, draws people back.

parallels.desc: slow to anger

verseByVerse.quote: But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God's righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works:
verseByVerse.commentary:
A hard, unrepentant heart stores up wrath for the day of judgment, when God will repay everyone according to their works.

Storing up. Like treasure, but its opposite.

The day of wrath. The final judgment.

According to his works. Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12. Judgment by works is consistent with justification by faith: works are the evidence of the heart (see vv. 7–8).

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

verseByVerse.quote: to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life; but for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who persevere in doing good, seeking glory, will receive eternal life; those who are self-seeking and reject the truth will face wrath.

Where Christians differ: what does Paul mean? Some read this as a hypothetical: if anyone perfectly did good, they would be saved, but no one does (3:10). Others see a real description of believers, whose Spirit-produced works are the evidence of faith at the judgment (8:4; Galatians 6:8). Verdict: the second fits Paul’s language of “seeking glory” and perseverance: the judgment publicly displays the faith that saves; it does not make works the ground of salvation (3:28).

Self-seeking. Selfish ambition, the opposite of seeking God’s glory.

verseByVerse.quote: There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek, but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s judgment is impartial: distress for every evildoer and glory for everyone who does good, Jew first and also Greek.

The Jew first. Greater privilege brings greater responsibility (Luke 12:48).

verseByVerse.quote: For God shows no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shows no favouritism.

Partiality. Literally “receiving the face”: judging by status or race (Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34).

For worship. Praise a Judge who cannot be bribed or impressed.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified. — Romans 2:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone will be judged by the light they had: those without the law apart from it, those with it by it; and only doers of the law are righteous.

Without the law. Gentiles are still accountable to conscience and creation.

Doers, not hearers. Owning the law does not save; keeping it is the standard, and no one fully does (3:20).

verseByVerse.quote: For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Gentiles without the law show by their conscience that God’s law is written on their hearts.

By nature. Common moral sense: most cultures condemn murder, theft and betrayal.

The work of the law on their hearts. Not the new covenant promise (Jeremiah 31:33), but the moral awareness given to all.

Where Christians differ. Some see these Gentiles as Gentile Christians. Most interpreters see the conscience of unbelievers. Inclusivists cite the passage as evidence that people may be saved by following conscience. Verdict: conscience proves accountability, not salvation; Paul concludes that all are under sin (3:9).

Accuse or excuse. Conscience is a witness, not a saviour.
verseByVerse.note: Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong that God has given to every person.

parallels.desc: I will write it on their hearts

verseByVerse.quote: on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day of judgment God will judge even the secrets of the heart, through Jesus Christ.

The secrets. Motives, private sins, hidden goodness (1 Corinthians 4:5).

By Christ Jesus. The judge is the Saviour (Acts 17:31).

According to my gospel. Judgment is part of the gospel message.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–29 — The Failure of Israel: Circumcision of the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now addresses the Jewish interlocutor directly, and the charge he levels is devastating. The Jew who possesses the Torah, who teaches it to others, who relies on it for his identity — does he keep it himself? "You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?" The indictment is not that the Torah is worthless but that it cannot save those who merely possess and teach it without obeying it from the heart.

The climax of the argument comes in the citation from Isaiah and Ezekiel: "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you." This is the ultimate indictment. Israel, entrusted with the oracles of God, called to be a light to the nations, had become in its hypocrisy a reason for the nations to despise the God of Israel. The covenant privilege had become a covenant disgrace. Nothing has changed in principle: every generation of the church must face the same charge — does our life commend the God we profess?

The solution Paul gestures toward is one of the most important concepts in the entire letter: "circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter" (v. 29). This is the Old Testament's own vision — Deuteronomy 10:16, Deuteronomy 30:6, Jeremiah 31:33, Ezekiel 36:26 — now being fulfilled in the new covenant. The mark of true belonging to God is not an outward physical sign but the inward transformation of the heart by the Spirit. This will be Paul's great theme in chapters 6–8.

One move in the middle of the section should not be passed over, because it is the sharpest thing in it. At verse 27 Paul does not merely say that circumcision without obedience is worthless. He says that the physically uncircumcised man who keeps the law will judge the man who has the letter, the circumcision, and a record of breaking it. The outsider is called as the prosecution witness. It is the same reversal our Lord made when he said of a Roman soldier that he had not found such faith in all Israel (Matthew 8:10), and it is designed to be intolerable to anyone whose security rests in the marking rather than in the obedience the marking was given to signify.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Purpose and Limits of the Law

Romans 2:17–29 is the first extended treatment of the law's purpose and limits in the letter. Calvin identified three uses of the law: to reveal sin, to restrain wickedness in society, and to guide the redeemed life. Paul is here invoking the first use: the law reveals sin. The Jew who possesses the Torah has a clearer mirror than the Gentile — and therefore a clearer sight of his own failure to meet its demands. The law cannot save; it can only expose the need for a Saviour. This is precisely why chapters 3–4 follow: the righteousness the law demands but cannot provide is given freely in the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish confidence in circumcision as the defining covenant mark was absolute in Paul's day. To question its saving significance was to question the entire structure of Second Temple Jewish identity. Paul does not question circumcision's historical significance; he relativises it entirely: the physical sign points to a spiritual reality, and when the sign is present without the reality, it is worse than useless. Now: The equivalent is any Christian community that trusts in the outward marks of religion — baptism, church attendance, doctrinal orthodoxy, moral reputation — as substitutes for the inward transformation of the heart by the Spirit. Paul's word stands: God looks at the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God and know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now addresses the Jew who relies on the law and boasts in God, privileges that are real.

Call yourself a Jew. A name of honour.

Rely on the law. As if possession protected.

Approve what is excellent. Instructed in God’s will.

verseByVerse.quote: and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jew rightly sees himself as a guide and teacher to the nations, as Israel was called to be.

A light to those in darkness. Israel’s vocation (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6).

The embodiment of knowledge. The law truly reveals God.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been called to be a light to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But teachers of the law who break it condemn themselves.

Teach yourself? Hypocrisy is the great danger of religious privilege.

Rob temples. Perhaps profiting from pagan temple goods, or robbing God of his due (Malachi 3:8).

On a Tuesday. If you teach Sunday school or lead a Bible study, practise first what you teach.

verseByVerse.quote: You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law.
verseByVerse.commentary: Boasting in the law while breaking it dishonours God.

verseByVerse.quote: For, as it is written, "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hypocrisy of God’s people causes his name to be blasphemed among the nations.

Isaiah 52:5; Ezekiel 36:20. Israel’s sin led to exile, and the nations mocked Israel’s God.

On a Tuesday. Christian hypocrisy still gives unbelievers reason to scoff. Your life is an advertisement for your Lord.

parallels.desc: my name is continually despised

verseByVerse.quote: For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Circumcision is valuable only if the law is kept; without obedience, it counts for nothing, and obedience without it counts as circumcision.

Of value. Circumcision was God’s covenant sign (Genesis 17).

Counted as circumcision. God looks for the reality, not merely the sign.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An uncircumcised person who keeps the law will condemn the circumcised lawbreaker.

Condemn you. As the Ninevites will condemn Jesus’ generation (Matthew 12:41).

verseByVerse.quote: For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. His praise is not from man but from God. — Romans 2:28–29
verseByVerse.commentary:
True Jewishness is inward: circumcision of the heart by the Spirit, which receives praise from God.

Inwardly. Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4: the prophets called for circumcised hearts.

By the Spirit, not the letter. New covenant renewal (2 Corinthians 3:6).

Praise from God. A wordplay: Jew comes from Judah, which means “praise”.

Applied to us. The same applies to baptism and church membership: the outward sign without the inward reality saves no one.

For worship. Ask God to give you a heart circumcised by his Spirit.

parallels.desc: the LORD will circumcise your heart

3.title: No One Righteous — But Now, Righteousness
3.overview:
Romans 3 is one of the most concentrated pieces of theological argument in the entire Bible. It moves through three distinct but connected moments: the faithfulness of God despite human faithlessness (vv. 1–8), the universal verdict of guilt on the entire human race from the Old Testament's own testimony (vv. 9–20), and then — with the two most beautiful words in the letter — "But now" (v. 21): the announcement of a righteousness from God that is apart from the law, given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe.

The emotional architecture of the chapter is deliberate. Paul has spent two chapters building the case for universal human guilt — the Gentile guilty through creation and conscience, the Jew guilty despite law and covenant. Now he delivers the verdict that springs from the evidence: no one righteous, not even one. And then, from within the deepest valley of human hopelessness, he sounds the trumpet of the gospel: the righteousness of God has been manifested. The darkness is real. The light is realer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — God's Faithfulness and Human Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If Jewish identity and covenant privilege provide no buffer against divine judgment (chapter 2), an obvious question arises: what advantage has the Jew? Was the entire covenant history of Israel pointless? Paul will not allow this conclusion. The advantage is real and great: "they were entrusted with the oracles of God." The Torah, the prophets, the promises — these are not nothing. They are the priceless repository of God's self-revelation and covenant purposes. The problem is not the oracles; the problem is the people who received them.

But what about God's faithfulness? If Israel has been faithless to the covenant, does that mean God's covenant promises have failed? Never, Paul declares — and the energy of his negation (mē genoito — "by no means!", "God forbid!", the strongest possible denial in Greek) is palpable. God's faithfulness is not contingent on human faithfulness. He remains true even when every human being is a liar. The covenant will not fail because the Covenant God cannot fail.

This brief passage anticipates the great argument of chapters 9–11: the apparent failure of Israel to embrace her Messiah does not represent a failure of God's word. His purposes stand. His faithfulness endures. The mystery of Israel's unbelief is not the defeat of God's plan but a part of it — and Paul will unfold that mystery with breathtaking scope later in the letter.

The second half of the section (vv. 5–8) turns to a pair of objections that Paul was evidently hearing in real life, and both are attempts to turn grace into a licence. If our unrighteousness only serves to display God’s righteousness more brightly, is God not unjust to punish it? And if my lie makes his truth more evident, why am I still condemned — why not simply “do evil that good may come”? Paul reports that last slander as something people were actually saying he taught, which tells us how radical his gospel of free grace sounded to its first hearers; no one ever accused the Pharisees of encouraging sin. He does not argue the point here — he refuses it, notes that God could judge nothing at all if the objection held, and reserves the full answer for chapter 6. But the objection itself is a compliment in disguise. A gospel that cannot be misheard as permission is probably not the gospel Paul preached.
verseByVerse.theology:
Divine Faithfulness and Human Failure

The question of whether human sin can thwart God's covenant purposes is one of the deepest in all theology. Romans 3:3–4 gives the Reformed answer: it cannot. God's faithfulness is not a function of human response; it is grounded in his own immutable character. Calvin wrote that God's truth stands firm even against the unfaithfulness of the whole world. This has practical implications for Christian assurance: our standing in the covenant does not rest on our faithfulness but on God's. He who called us is faithful; he will do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish readers would have been relieved by Paul's affirmation of Israel's covenant privileges, but troubled by his insistence that these privileges provide no exemption from judgment. The tension — covenant advantage, yet equal accountability — was genuinely new, though rooted in the Old Testament prophets. Now: Christians face the same tension. The advantages of covenant community — Scripture, sacrament, preaching, prayer — are real and great. They are also not saving substitutes for personal faith and repentance. Privilege and accountability always travel together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being a Jew is a great privilege, above all because Israel was entrusted with the very words of God.

What advantage? Paul anticipates the objection that chapter 2 has made Jewishness worthless.

The oracles of God. The Scriptures. Israel’s greatest privilege was the word (9:4–5).

On a Tuesday. If you have a Bible in your language, you share that privilege. Do not waste it.
verseByVerse.note: “The oracles of God” are the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, "That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Human unfaithfulness cannot cancel God’s faithfulness: God remains true even if every person is a liar.

Let God be true. God’s integrity is the fixed point.

Psalm 51:4. David confessed that God is justified when he judges.

For worship. Praise the God who keeps his word even when we do not.

parallels.desc: so that you may be justified in your words
all mankind are liars

verseByVerse.quote: But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.) By no means! For then how could God judge the world?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If our sin shows off God’s righteousness, it does not follow that God is unjust to punish it.

Speaking in a human way. Paul voices a bad argument in order to refute it.

How could God judge the world? If God could not punish sin, he could not be the judge of all the earth (Genesis 18:25).

parallels.desc: shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?

verseByVerse.quote: But if through my lie God's truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? And why not do evil that good may come? — as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Their condemnation is just.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Doing evil so that good may come is a slander on the gospel, and those who say it are justly condemned.

Slanderously charged. Paul’s opponents said his gospel of grace encouraged sin (6:1).

Their condemnation is just. Grace never excuses sin.

On a Tuesday. If your understanding of grace makes sin seem less serious, you have misunderstood grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — No One Is Righteous: The Verdict of Scripture
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul has argued the guilt of the Gentile from creation and conscience. He has argued the guilt of the moralist and the Jew from their own failure to live by the law they possess. Now he seals the case with the testimony of Israel's own scriptures. The catena of Old Testament citations in vv. 10–18 — drawn from Psalms 14, 5, 140, 10, 36, and Isaiah 59 — forms a comprehensive indictment: no one is righteous, no one understands, no one seeks God; their throats are open graves, their mouths full of cursing and bitterness, their feet swift to shed blood, and there is no fear of God before their eyes.

The theological move is masterful. Paul is not importing foreign charges against Israel; he is using Israel's own sacred texts to establish Israel's own guilt. The Torah was given to the Jew; and the Torah says that no one is righteous. Therefore the Jew who trusts in the Torah as a source of righteousness has not read the Torah carefully enough. The law's purpose is not to provide righteousness but to reveal the absence of it: "through the law comes knowledge of sin" (v. 20).

"No one" — the universality is relentless. Not most people. Not unreformed people. Not people without religion. No one. The scope of the verdict prepares for the scope of the remedy: the gospel is for everyone because everyone needs it equally. There are no moral high achievers who need it slightly less. There are no spiritual derelicts for whom it is too late. The ground is completely level: all have sinned, all fall short (v. 23), all are justified freely by grace (v. 24).

And the section closes with a courtroom image worth naming, because it is the most vivid thing in it. The purpose of the whole indictment, Paul says, is “so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God” (v. 19). A stopped mouth is what happens at the end of a trial that has gone badly: the defendant who arrived with explanations has run out of them, and the silence in the dock is the verdict arriving before the judge speaks it. That silence is not the aim of the passage but its precondition — because a man still talking is a man still defending himself, and nobody has ever been justified by grace while he was still presenting a case.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity

Romans 3:9–20 is the locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of total depravity. The doctrine does not mean that every human being is as bad as possible, but that sin has corrupted every dimension of human nature — the mind ("no one understands"), the will ("no one seeks for God"), the affections, the speech, the conduct, the very orientation of the soul. No part of the human person is untouched by the fall. This means that the human contribution to salvation is precisely zero: we do not contribute our goodwill, our moral achievement, our religious sensitivity. Salvation is entirely of God from beginning to end. This is why Paul can say in v. 24 that justification is "freely" given — there is nothing in us to which it could be a response.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The catena of psalms and prophets Paul deploys was drawn from Israel's own worship book. These were texts sung in the temple, prayed in the synagogue, memorised by devout Jews. Their application to Israel's own guilt was deeply confrontational — like a church being indicted by its own hymns. Now: The contemporary church sometimes prefers a more optimistic anthropology — emphasising human potential and the image of God while minimising the ravages of the fall. Romans 3:9–20 is the permanent corrective. The doctrine of human depravity is not pessimism; it is realism. And realism about the disease is the precondition for gratitude for the cure.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin, as it is written: "None is righteous, no, not one;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jews are no better off before God than Gentiles: all alike are under the power of sin.

Under sin. Not just guilty of sins, but enslaved to sin’s power.

None righteous. Psalm 14:1–3; 53:1–3. A chain of Old Testament quotations follows.
verseByVerse.note: Paul strings together quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah to show that all are under sin.

parallels.desc: not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins

verseByVerse.quote: no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one naturally understands or seeks God; everyone has turned aside.

No one seeks. People seek religion, meaning or help, but not the true God on his terms (John 6:44). Where anyone seeks him, God sought first.

Worthless. Gone sour, like spoilt milk.

Where Christians differ: total depravity. See the note on Ephesians 2:1. Verdict: every part of human nature is affected by sin, so that no one can turn to God without his grace.

verseByVerse.quote: "Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive." "The venom of asps is under their lips." "Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin poisons our speech: throat, tongue, lips and mouth.

Psalm 5:9; 140:3; 10:7. Speech reveals the heart (Matthew 12:34).

parallels.desc: their throat is an open grave
the venom of asps
his mouth is filled with cursing

verseByVerse.quote: "Their feet are swift to shed blood;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin leads quickly to violence.

Isaiah 59:7. Swift to shed blood.

parallels.desc: their feet run to evil

verseByVerse.quote: "in their paths are ruin and misery, and the way of peace they have not known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin leaves a trail of ruin, and knows nothing of peace.

Isaiah 59:7–8. Every road of the sinner ends in misery.

parallels.desc: the way of peace they do not know

verseByVerse.quote: "There is no fear of God before their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The root of all sin is the absence of the fear of God.

Psalm 36:1. No reverence for God, so no restraint.

On a Tuesday. The fear of the Lord is not terror but reverent awe that shapes decisions (Proverbs 1:7).

parallels.desc: there is no fear of God before his eyes

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin. — Romans 3:19-20
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law silences every mouth and holds the whole world accountable, because by works of the law no one will be justified; the law brings knowledge of sin.

Every mouth stopped. No defence remains.

No flesh justified. Psalm 143:2.

Knowledge of sin. The law is a mirror, not a washbasin.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — But Now: The Righteousness of God Through Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"But now" — nuni de. Two words in Greek that change everything. After three chapters of unrelenting diagnosis — the Gentile without excuse, the moralist self-condemned, the Jew convicted by his own scriptures, the entire world accountable to God — these two words open a door out of a sealed room. The righteousness of God has been manifested. Apart from the law. Through faith in Jesus Christ. For all who believe. Freely. By grace. Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

This is the centre of Romans. This is the centre of Paul's gospel. This is the theological core of the Reformation. Every word of vv. 21–26 has been weighed and debated and celebrated for two millennia — and still it burns with the same fire. God put Christ forward as a propitiation — a mercy seat, a place of atonement — by his blood, to be received by faith. In this act, God demonstrated his own righteousness: He passed over former sins (under the patient forbearance of the old covenant) and he condemned the sin that deserved condemnation — in his own Son, at Calvary. The God who justifies the ungodly (4:5) is not a God who winks at sin. He is a God who bore its full weight in the person of his Son.

Boasting is excluded (v. 27). The person who is justified by faith through Christ has nothing to boast of but Christ. The Jew cannot boast in the Torah; the Greek cannot boast in philosophy; the moralist cannot boast in her record; the religious cannot boast in his devotion. The ground is level. There is one God, and he justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. The gospel is the great leveller — and the great glorifier, because it redirects all glory from the creature to the Creator.

Two things at the edges of the section should not be lost. The first is the sentence on which the whole offer rests, and it is the shortest in the passage: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (v. 23). It is not an insult dropped into a paragraph about grace; it is the reason there is a paragraph about grace, and everything from 1:18 onward has been written to make that sentence land as a plain description rather than an accusation. The second is the question Paul asks last, which is the one his critics had been asking loudly: do we then overthrow the law by this faith (v. 31)? He has just said righteousness comes apart from the law, and the obvious inference is that the law has been discarded — the very charge of 3:8. His answer is the strongest denial in his vocabulary, and then four words that will take him the whole of chapter 4 to prove: we uphold the law. Justification by faith does not abolish the Old Testament. It is what the Old Testament was about.
verseByVerse.theology:
Propitiation: The Heart of the Atonement

Romans 3:25 introduces one of the most important words in the New Testament: hilastērion — propitiation. This word carries the specific meaning of an offering that averts divine wrath by satisfying it. Leon Morris demonstrated exhaustively that this is the correct reading against C.H. Dodd's attempted substitution of "expiation" (which only removes sin, without reference to wrath). Christ's death on the cross was not merely a moral demonstration or a removal of guilt; it was the bearing of the holy wrath of God against sin, so that God could be both just (the sin was punished) and the justifier (the sinner is acquitted). The Reformed tradition has always insisted on this: without propitiation, justification has no foundation. If the wrath was not truly satisfied, the forgiveness is not truly free.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The language of vv. 24–25 deliberately echoes the Day of Atonement ritual of Leviticus 16: the mercy seat (hilastērion) where blood was sprinkled to cover the sins of the people. Paul is saying: what the Day of Atonement pointed to, Christ has accomplished — once for all, for all who believe. The entire sacrificial system of the old covenant found its fulfilment and its terminus in the cross. Now: Every human religion has some mechanism for dealing with the problem of guilt — sacrifice, ritual, moral achievement, reincarnation, denial. Romans 3:21–31 announces that the only mechanism that actually works is the one God provided: the substitutionary death of his own Son, received by faith. There is no other name, no other blood, no other righteousness that avails.

verseByVerse.quote: But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it—the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction:
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now, apart from the law, God has revealed a righteousness, witnessed by the Scriptures, given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe.

But now. The turning point of the letter.

Apart from the law. Not earned by law-keeping.

The Law and the Prophets. The Old Testament testifies to it (Genesis 15:6; Habakkuk 2:4).

Through faith in Jesus Christ. Or “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ”. Verdict: “for all who believe” immediately follows, so faith in Christ is in view, resting on his faithfulness.

No distinction. Jew and Gentile alike.
verseByVerse.note: To be “justified” is to be declared righteous by God as judge.

verseByVerse.quote: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
All have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, and all who believe are declared righteous freely by his grace, through the redemption in Christ Jesus.

All have sinned. The universal diagnosis.

Fall short. Present tense: we keep falling short of the glory we were made to reflect.

Justified. Declared righteous, a legal verdict, not made righteous by inner change (though that follows).

As a gift by his grace. Freely, without cost to us.

Redemption. Release by payment (Mark 10:45).

Where Christians differ: justification. Roman Catholic teaching includes inner renewal in justification. The Reformers held it to be a declaration based on Christ’s righteousness imputed to the believer. Verdict: justification by faith alone, a legal verdict; sanctification follows inseparably.
verseByVerse.note: “Redemption” was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: ...whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. — Romans 3:25-26
verseByVerse.commentary:
God presented Christ as the sacrifice that turns away his wrath, received through faith, to show that he is both just and the one who justifies those who believe in Jesus.

Propitiation. Hilastērion, the mercy seat in the tabernacle, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Where Christians differ. Some (C. H. Dodd) translated it “expiation”, removing sin, to avoid the idea of God’s wrath. Others (Leon Morris) showed that the word includes turning away wrath (1:18). Verdict: propitiation: Christ’s death satisfied God’s justice and turned away his wrath, as well as removing sin.

Passed over former sins. God’s forbearance before the cross might have seemed unjust; the cross shows he dealt with them.

Just and justifier. The heart of the gospel: God does not overlook sin; he punishes it in Christ, and can therefore acquit the guilty without compromising his justice.

For worship. Stand amazed: the Judge has paid your penalty himself.
verseByVerse.note: A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. The same word is used in the Greek Old Testament for the “mercy seat,” the lid of the ark where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement.

parallels.desc: blood on the mercy seat

verseByVerse.quote: Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boasting is excluded, because a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.

A law of faith. The principle of faith.

Apart from works. Luther translated “by faith alone” (allein durch den Glauben), which was criticised as an addition, but it states the meaning exactly: if apart from works, then by faith alone.

On a Tuesday. Nothing you do today will make God love you more. Do good anyway, out of gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one—who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since there is only one God, he justifies Jew and Gentile alike, on the same basis: faith.

One God. The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) means one Saviour for all peoples.
verseByVerse.note: “God is one” echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession.

parallels.desc: the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith does not overthrow the law; it establishes it.

Uphold the law. The gospel fulfils what the law pointed to, satisfies its demands in Christ, and produces obedience by the Spirit (8:4). Chapter 4 shows how the law itself, in Abraham’s story, teaches justification by faith.
