7.title: The Law, the Flesh, and the Struggle Within
7.overview:
Romans 7 is one of the most debated chapters in the New Testament. The first six verses use the analogy of marriage to explain the Christian's release from the law — just as death dissolves a marriage, so the death of the old self has dissolved the law's claim on the believer. Verses 7–25 then address the relationship between the law and sin in a passage of such raw psychological honesty that it has divided interpreters for centuries: is Paul describing his experience before or after his conversion?

The Reformed tradition, following Luther and Calvin, has generally argued that vv. 7–25 describe the experience of the regenerate person — not as the normal steady state of the mature Christian, but as the honest account of the ongoing struggle that even the believer has with indwelling sin. The person who says "I delight in the law of God in my inner being" (v. 22) is not an unregenerate person; the unregenerate person has no such delight. The chapter is not a counsel of despair but a radical honesty about the nature of the Christian struggle — which ends, in v. 25, with the triumphant answer: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Released from the Law to Bear Fruit for God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul uses the analogy of marriage to make a point about the law's jurisdiction. A woman is bound to her husband by law as long as he lives; if he dies, she is free to marry another. In the same way, the Christian has "died" to the law through her union with Christ's death — she is no longer bound to the law as a system of earning and condemnation. She is now married to another — to Christ who was raised from the dead — so that she might bear fruit for God.

The point is not that the law is bad (v. 7 will explicitly deny this) but that the law was never the instrument of life. Under the law's jurisdiction, the sinful passions "aroused by the law were at work in our members to bear fruit for death" (v. 5). This does not mean the law created those sinful passions; it means that the sinful nature, encountering prohibition, is provoked — not helped — by the law. The law reveals and aggravates what is already there; it cannot remove it.

But now — freed from the law, joined to Christ — the Christian serves "in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code" (v. 6). This is not antinomianism; it is the fulfilment of Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 — the new covenant in which the law is written on the heart by the Spirit, not merely imposed from without by the letter. The motive for obedience has changed: from fear of penalty to love of the God who has shown such grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Death to Law: Liberation for Obedience

The believer's death to the law (vv. 4, 6) has been the source of great misunderstanding. Paul is not teaching that the Christian is released from the moral content of the law — he will demonstrate in chapters 12–15 that the redeemed life is the life of love, which is the fulfilment of the law (13:8–10). He is teaching that the believer's relationship to the law has changed: no longer subject to it as a court that condemns, the Christian is now free to embrace its moral demands as the expression of the will of the God she loves. Calvin's third use of the law: a guide for the regenerate, not a goad for the condemned.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The marriage analogy was immediately accessible to Paul's Jewish readers, for whom marriage law was well understood. The death that dissolves the marriage — the death of the old self in union with Christ's death — was the theologically startling element. Paul is saying: you belong to a new husband now. The old master (law as condemning power) is dead to you; the new master (Christ) is alive to you. Serve him accordingly. Now: Many Christians live as though they are still married to the law — haunted by condemnation, driven by religious duty, exhausted by the performance of obligation. Romans 7:1–6 is the declaration of liberty: you have died to that system. You are joined to Christ. Serve him from love, not from fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know, brothers — for I am speaking to those who know the law — that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law has authority over a person only while that person lives.

Those who know the law. Jewish and God-fearing believers.

Bound by law. Marriage illustrates it: the bond lasts until death.

parallels.desc: a wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A married woman who joins another man while her husband lives commits adultery, but she is free if he dies.

The illustration. Not teaching on divorce, but showing that death ends legal obligation.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God. For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers have died to the law through Christ’s body, so that they belong to the risen Christ and bear fruit for God.

Died to the law. Through union with Christ’s death (Galatians 2:19).

Belong to another. Married to Christ.

In the flesh. Before conversion, the law aroused sinful passions.

verseByVerse.quote: But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Released from the law, believers serve in the new way of the Spirit, not the old way of the written code.

The new way of the Spirit. Obedience from a renewed heart (2 Corinthians 3:6).

What it does not mean. Not lawlessness: the Spirit writes God’s law on the heart (8:4).

parallels.desc: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–25 — The Law and the Ongoing Conflict
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means!" Paul's defence of the law is passionate and complete: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good (v. 12). The problem is not the law; the problem is sin — which used the good commandment as a foothold for its own agenda. When the commandment "you shall not covet" entered Paul's consciousness, it awakened the very covetousness it forbade. Not because the commandment was defective, but because sin is so pervasive that even the confrontation with prohibition provokes the prohibited desire.

The famous passage beginning in v. 14 — "For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate" — is the most honest description of the experience of indwelling sin in all of Scripture. Whether Paul is describing pre-conversion or post-conversion experience has been debated exhaustively. The weight of the evidence — the delight in God's law (v. 22), the willing of the good (v. 18), the self-awareness of the conflict — points to the regenerate person, not the unregenerate.

The climax of the chapter is both a cry and a triumph: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" (vv. 24–25). The cry of anguish is honest; the gratitude that follows is immediate. Paul does not wallow in the wretchedness. He knows the answer. He has the answer. The very struggle he describes is the evidence that the Spirit is at work — because the person without the Spirit does not experience this conflict; she simply does what sin desires. The one who hates what she does and loves the law of God in her inner being is alive in Christ, even while she wars against the flesh.

Two things in the middle of the chapter carry the argument and should not be lost. The first is Paul’s conclusion at v. 13, which is the point of the whole autobiographical section: the law did not kill him, sin did — working death in him through what is good, so that sin might be shown to be sin and might become sinful beyond measure. That is the purpose of the exercise. The law was given partly to provoke sin into the open, where its true character could be seen; a disease that is invisible cannot be treated, and sin’s worst feature is exactly its capacity to use a holy commandment as its instrument. The second is the image at v. 23, which supplies the vocabulary for everything Christians have said since about the inner conflict: another law waging war against the law of the mind, and taking the man captive. Paul does not describe an imbalance or a tension. He describes a campaign, with two sides, prisoners, and territory — which is why the chapter can end in a cry rather than a conclusion.
verseByVerse.theology:
Indwelling Sin and the Doctrine of Sanctification

Romans 7:14–25 is the biblical foundation for the Reformed doctrine that sanctification is a lifelong struggle, not a crisis experience of eradication. John Wesley and the Holiness tradition argued for the possibility of entire sanctification — the complete eradication of the sinful nature — in this life. The Reformed tradition, following Augustine, Luther, and Calvin, has insisted that indwelling sin remains until glorification. This is not defeatism but realism: the Christian who understands this will not be surprised or destroyed by the ongoing struggle. She will be equipped to fight it with the means God has provided — the Word, prayer, the sacraments, the community of believers — rather than pretending it does not exist or despairing when it does.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The experience Paul describes in vv. 14–25 had a parallel in the literature of the day — Ovid's famous line, spoken by Medea: "I see the better and approve it; I follow the worse." But the philosophers' solution (more reason, more discipline, more willpower) is precisely what Paul finds inadequate. The problem is not ignorance; it is the power of indwelling sin that reason alone cannot overcome. The solution is not philosophy; it is the liberating power of "Jesus Christ our Lord" (v. 25). Now: The Christian who has experienced Romans 7 — who has tried harder, prayed more, committed afresh, and still found the same sins returning — is not a failure. She is a normal Christian, living in the honest tension between the new self and the old, between the delight in God's law and the drag of indwelling sin. The answer is not more effort; it is more Christ. Chapter 8 is the answer to chapter 7.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, "You shall not covet." But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is not sin; it exposed sin, and sin used the commandment to stir up every kind of desire.

Covet. The tenth commandment reaches the heart, where outward obedience cannot hide.

An opportunity. A base of operations: sin twists a good command into a provocation.
verseByVerse.note: Coveting is the one commandment that concerns only the heart.

parallels.desc: you shall not covet

verseByVerse.quote: I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the commandment came, sin sprang to life and Paul died: the command meant for life brought death.

Who is “I”? Where scholars differ. Paul’s own experience, perhaps as a boy coming under the law; Adam in Eden; or Israel at Sinai. Verdict: Paul speaks personally but representatively, echoing Adam’s story.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin deceived and killed through the commandment; the law itself is holy, righteous and good.

Deceived. As the serpent deceived Eve (Genesis 3:13).

Holy, righteous and good. The problem is not the law but sin.
verseByVerse.note: “Deceived” echoes the serpent’s deception of Eve.

parallels.desc: the serpent deceived me

verseByVerse.quote: Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good law did not cause death; sin did, using the law, and so sin was shown to be utterly sinful.

Sinful beyond measure. The law unmasks sin’s true nature.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is spiritual, but Paul is of the flesh, sold under sin, and he does not do what he wants.

Where Christians differ: who speaks in 7:14–25? Some (many early fathers, Arminians and some modern scholars) read this as an unbeliever or a believer before the Spirit (contrast 8:1–2). Augustine (later), Luther, Calvin and many Reformed read it as the mature Christian, who delights in God’s law yet still struggles with sin. Verdict: the Christian: present tense, delight in the law (v. 22) and service of the law with the mind (v. 25) mark a regenerate person; but the passage describes the struggle viewed from the law’s side, and chapter 8 gives the Spirit’s victory.

Sold under sin. Sin’s presence still holds sway in the flesh.
verseByVerse.note: Christians have long debated whether Paul here describes life before conversion or the ongoing struggle of a believer; many, following Augustine and the Reformers, read it as the believer’s experience.

parallels.desc: the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Doing what he hates shows that Paul agrees the law is good, and that indwelling sin is at work.

No longer I. Not an excuse, but a distinction between the true self and indwelling sin.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing good lives in the flesh: Paul wants to do right but cannot carry it out.

In my flesh. Paul qualifies: not in the new self.

The will without the power. Honest realism about the Christian life.

On a Tuesday. If you hate your sin and fight it, that is a sign of new life, not its absence.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, not the body as such.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary: When evil is present even as he wants to do good, Paul recognises a law at work: indwelling sin.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his inner being Paul delights in God’s law, but another law wages war in his body.

Delight. Only a renewed heart delights in God’s law (Psalm 1:2; 119:97).

At war. The battle between Spirit and flesh (Galatians 5:17).

parallels.desc: his delight is in the law of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cry of the struggling believer, “Who will rescue me?”, is answered with thanks to God through Jesus Christ.

Wretched man. Not despair, but honest lament.

This body of death. Mortal life under sin.

Thanks be to God. Rescue now (8:1–4) and finally in the resurrection (8:23).

So then. The two-sided reality continues until glory.

For worship. Bring your struggle to God, and thank him for Jesus Christ.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Or do you not know, brothers —for I am speaking to those who know the law—that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives?<sup>2</sup>For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.<sup>3</sup>Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.<sup>4</sup>Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God.<sup>5</sup>For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.<sup>6</sup>But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.<sup>7</sup>What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.”<sup>8</sup>But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.<sup>9</sup>I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died.<sup>10</sup>The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.<sup>11</sup>For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.<sup>12</sup>So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.<sup>13</sup>Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.<sup>14</sup>For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin.<sup>15</sup>For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.<sup>16</sup>Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good.<sup>17</sup>So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.<sup>18</sup>For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out.<sup>19</sup>For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.<sup>20</sup>Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.<sup>21</sup>So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.<sup>22</sup>For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being,<sup>23</sup>but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.<sup>24</sup>Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?<sup>25</sup>Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.

8.title: No Condemnation, All Glory
8.overview:
Romans 8 is the mountain peak of the New Testament. Commentators across twenty centuries have reached for superlatives and still found them inadequate. It begins with "no condemnation" and ends with "no separation" — and between those two impossibilities of loss, it contains the fullest and most glorious account of the Christian life available in Scripture: the Spirit, adoption, the groaning of creation, the golden chain of redemption, and the love of God from which nothing in the universe can separate us.

The movement of the chapter is from liberation (vv. 1–17) through present suffering (vv. 18–27) to eternal security (vv. 28–39). In each movement, the Spirit is central: He liberates (vv. 1–11), he adopts (vv. 14–17), he intercedes (vv. 26–27). And over all of it stands the sovereign love of a God who foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and will glorify — a chain that has never had a broken link and never will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — No Condemnation: Life in the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." One sentence — and the whole of the gospel's comfort is here. Not less condemnation. Not reduced condemnation. No condemnation. The verdict is absolute, unconditional, and permanent. It rests not on the quality of the believer's life on any given day but on the finished work of Christ and the irreversible union with him by faith.

The reason for the "no condemnation" is the "law of the Spirit of life" which has set the believer free from "the law of sin and death" (v. 2). This is not two different legal codes but two different powers — the power of the Spirit that gives life versus the power of sin that produces death. Christ condemned sin in the flesh (v. 3) — He bore its penalty, exhausted its power, stripped it of its right to condemn — so that the Spirit-empowered believer might fulfil the righteous requirement of the law (v. 4).

The contrast between "flesh" and "Spirit" in vv. 5–11 is not between body and soul — Paul is not a Gnostic. It is between life oriented around the self and its capacities (flesh) and life oriented around God and his Spirit (Spirit). The mind set on the flesh is death; the mind set on the Spirit is life and peace. The Christian is not defined by the flesh but by the Spirit — "you, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you" (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Definitive Justification and Ongoing Assurance

Romans 8:1 is the permanent foundation of the Reformed doctrine of assurance. The condemnation that does not exist for those in Christ is not merely past (sins before conversion) but total: nothing from the past, present, or future can generate condemnation for the one who is in Christ. This is because justification is not a process but an event — a forensic declaration that has been made and cannot be unmade. The Christian may sin grievously; she is not beyond discipline, but she is not in danger of condemnation. The Spirit she has received is the guarantee (v. 11) that what began in justification will be completed in glorification.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jewish legal system that Paul's readers knew well had a concept of condemnation — the verdict of guilty rendered by a court against one who had violated the law. Paul takes this forensic language and applies it to the ultimate court: the tribunal of God. The verdict of "no condemnation" is the legal declaration of the divine Judge that the case is closed, the penalty has been paid, and the accused walks free — permanently. Now: Countless Christians live under a cloud of functional condemnation — not doubting their doctrinal justification but unable to feel free, perpetually haunted by past sins, unable to receive grace without qualifying it. Romans 8:1 is the word that cuts through all of this: not less condemnation, not reduced condemnation — none. Take it in. Live from it.

verseByVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death. — Romans 8:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who are in Christ face no condemnation, because the Spirit of life has set them free from the law of sin and death.

Therefore now. The answer to the cry of 7:24.

No condemnation. Not less condemnation, but none (8:33–34).

In Christ Jesus. Union with Christ is the ground.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit” (KJV), copied from verse 4. Verdict: not original here; no condemnation rests on Christ, not on our walk.

For worship. Read the verse aloud, and believe it about yourself.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who walk not according to the flesh,” and that some read “me” for “you.”

verseByVerse.quote: For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. — Romans 8:3–4
verseByVerse.commentary:
What the law could not do, God did: he sent his Son as a sin offering and condemned sin in his flesh, so that the law’s righteous requirement is fulfilled in us who walk by the Spirit.

Weakened by the flesh. The law’s weakness is our sinfulness.

In the likeness of sinful flesh. Truly human, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

For sin. As a sin offering (Leviticus 4).

Condemned sin in the flesh. Sin was judged in Christ’s body on the cross.

Fulfilled in us. Not by us earning, but by the Spirit producing obedience.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “for sin” can also be rendered “as a sin offering.”

parallels.desc: the sin offering

verseByVerse.quote: For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit. For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What we set our minds on reveals whether we belong to the flesh or the Spirit, and leads either to death or to life and peace.

Set their minds. A whole outlook, not passing thoughts.

On a Tuesday. What does your mind return to when it is free? That is the clue.

verseByVerse.quote: For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mind set on the flesh is hostile to God, will not submit to his law and cannot please him.

Cannot. Inability, not just unwillingness: the doctrine of total depravity (John 6:44).

verseByVerse.quote: You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every believer has the Spirit of Christ; anyone without him does not belong to Christ.

The Spirit of God, the Spirit of Christ. The same Spirit: a pointer to Christ’s deity and to the Spirit’s procession from the Son.

Does not belong to him. There are no Christians without the Spirit, and no second-class believers.

The body dead, the spirit alive. Our bodies still die because of sin, but our spirits live because of righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit who raised Jesus lives in believers and will raise their mortal bodies too.

Will also give life. Bodily resurrection is guaranteed by the Spirit’s presence now.

The Trinity in a verse. The Father raised Jesus; the Spirit dwells; the Christ is the firstborn.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Heirs with Christ: The Spirit of Adoption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit does not merely set us free from condemnation; he establishes our identity as children of God. "For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'" (v. 15). The word Abba is the intimate Aramaic term for father — the word a child uses at the family table, in the moment of fear, in the unselfconscious familiarity of the parental relationship. Jesus used it in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). His Spirit now enables his adopted brothers and sisters to use it too.

The adoption of which Paul speaks is not merely a legal status (though it is that — full legal rights as sons and daughters, co-heirs with Christ). It is a relational reality experienced in the present: the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. This inner witness — not our feelings but the Spirit's testimony — is the ground of Christian assurance at the deepest level. When we doubt our standing, when darkness presses in, when God feels distant — the Spirit within is still crying "Abba!" on our behalf.

"Heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ" (v. 17) — the inheritance is nothing less than God himself, shared with the Son. Everything that belongs to Christ by right of his eternal sonship is ours by right of our adoption. This is the logic behind Paul's bewildering statement in 1 Corinthians 3:21 — "all things are yours." The adopted child of God is heir to a universe, co-inheritor of a new creation. The suffering of the present age (v. 17 — "provided we suffer with him") is the path to that glory, not its obstacle.

The section does not begin there, however, and the two verses that open it are the hinge on which the rest turns. Paul first cancels an obligation: we are debtors — but not to the flesh. The old master has no further claim, which means every demand it still makes is made without authority. Then comes the one command in the passage, and it is not gentle: by the Spirit, put to death the deeds of the body (v. 13). This is the letter’s answer to the defeat of chapter 7, and it holds two things together that we habitually separate — the killing is genuinely ours to do, and the power to do it is not ours at all. And verse 14 then supplies the link to everything that follows: those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. The mortification of sin is not the price of sonship. It is the evidence of it, and the family likeness of people who are being led.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption and Assurance

The doctrine of adoption (huiothesia) is one of J.I. Packer's great themes in Knowing God: he argues that adoption is a higher privilege than justification, because justification changes our status before the court while adoption brings us into the family. Reformed writing on the Holy Spirit develops the same insight: the Spirit's primary work in the believer is to mediate the Trinitarian relationship — drawing the child into the love that the Father and the Son share, enabling her to cry "Abba" with the same intimacy that the eternal Son has always known. Assurance, at its deepest level, is not confidence in our own faith or our own experience; it is the Spirit-given knowledge that we are beloved children of the Father.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman adoption law in the first century was clear: an adopted son received full legal rights, the old debts were cancelled, the new family name was his, and the inheritance was secured. Paul's readers would have understood immediately the thoroughness of what adoption meant. No second-class status, no probationary period — full sonship, full inheritance, from the moment of adoption. Now: The "spirit of slavery" (v. 15) that produces fear is the functional religion of much nominal Christianity — the haunting sense that God is primarily a demanding judge to be appeased, that our standing depends on our performance, that we must earn our place at the table. Romans 8:15 is the antidote: not slaves, sons. Not fear, Abba. Not earning, inheriting.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. — Romans 8:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
We owe the flesh nothing; by the Spirit we must keep putting to death the deeds of the body, and we will live.

Debtors. Our obligation is to the Spirit.

Put to death. Mortification: a daily, active killing of sin (Colossians 3:5). John Owen: be killing sin or it will be killing you.

By the Spirit. Not willpower alone.

parallels.desc: put to death what is earthly in you

verseByVerse.quote: For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, "Abba! Father!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those led by the Spirit are God’s sons, and he gives them not a spirit of slavish fear but of adoption, by which they cry “Abba! Father!”

Led by the Spirit. In the context, led into the fight against sin, not mainly into decisions.

Adoption. Full sonship (Galatians 4:5–7).

Abba. Intimate trust.
verseByVerse.note: In Roman law an adopted son received full rights and inheritance, as if born into the family. “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

parallels.desc: sons of the living God

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit himself confirms to our spirit that we are God’s children.

Bears witness with. The Spirit testifies alongside our own awareness, through the word and through the cry of “Abba”.

Where Christians differ: assurance. Rome (Trent) denied that ordinary believers can have certain assurance of salvation without special revelation. The Reformers taught that assurance is possible and normal, grounded in God’s promises, confirmed by the Spirit’s witness and the evidence of grace (Westminster Confession 18). Verdict: believers may and should be assured.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him. — Romans 8:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
As God’s children, believers are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, sharing his sufferings now so as to share his glory.

Heirs of God. God himself is our inheritance.

Suffer with him. Suffering is the normal path to glory, not a sign of God’s absence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Future Glory: Groaning, Intercession, and the Golden Chain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The present sufferings are real — Paul does not minimise them — but they are not worth comparing to the glory that is to be revealed (v. 18). The entire creation groans, longing for the liberation that the resurrection of the children of God will bring. The believer groans too, in the Spirit, longing for the full redemption of the body. And the Spirit himself groans on behalf of believers with groanings too deep for words, interceding according to the will of God. Three levels of groaning: creation, believer, Spirit — all pointed toward the same consummation: the full glory of the children of God in the new creation.

"And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (v. 28). This verse has comforted more afflicted souls than almost any other in Scripture — and it has been more abused by careless application than almost any other. Paul is not promising that everything that happens to Christians will feel good or produce obvious benefit. He is promising that the God who is sovereign over all things is working in all things — the good and the bad, the joyful and the painful — toward a single end: the good of those he has called. The suffering is not outside his purposes; it is within them.

The "golden chain" of vv. 29–30 is the most concise summary of the Reformed ordo salutis in Scripture: foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified. Five links, each leading inevitably to the next, with no link missing and none reversible. The glorification is in the past tense — "he also glorified" — because it is as certain as if it had already happened. The God who foreknew in eternity past will glorify in eternity future, and nothing can interrupt the chain.
verseByVerse.theology:
Effectual Calling and the Golden Chain

Romans 8:29–30 is the biblical foundation for the Reformed doctrine of election and effectual calling. Foreknowledge here is not merely prior knowledge but prior relational knowing — the same sense in which God "knew" Israel (Amos 3:2) or the Shepherd knows his sheep (John 10:14). Those whom God foreknew with this special, electing love he predestined; those he predestined he called (effectually, inwardly, irresistibly); those he called he justified; those he justified he glorified. The chain is unbreakable. Every link is divine. The reason no one finally falls from grace is not that believers are strong enough to hold on, but that the God who foreknew and called them is powerful enough to keep what he has started.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The groaning of creation in vv. 19–22 draws on the Jewish understanding that the natural world was affected by human sin (Genesis 3:17–18) and will be renewed in the messianic age. Paul extends this vision: not just Israel but the whole creation waits for the redemption of God's children. The gospel is not merely the rescue of souls; it is the renewal of all things. Now: Romans 8:28 is one of the most misused verses in the Christian repertoire — invoked as a quick comfort for minor inconveniences and sometimes grotesquely applied to genuine catastrophe. Used rightly, it is not a promise that things will work out the way we hope; it is the promise of a sovereign God who is working toward his purpose in all things — and his purpose is better than our preferences.

verseByVerse.quote: For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us.

I consider. A calculation: Paul has weighed both.

Not worth comparing. No contest (2 Corinthians 4:17).

On a Tuesday. Hold your heaviest trouble against eternity, and let it shrink.

verseByVerse.quote: For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole creation longs eagerly for the day God’s children are revealed, because it was subjected to frustration.

Creation. The non-human world.

Subjected to futility. By God, after the fall (Genesis 3:17–19).

In hope. The curse was never the last word.
verseByVerse.note: The creation was subjected to futility when God cursed the ground after Adam’s sin.

parallels.desc: cursed is the ground because of you

verseByVerse.quote: that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Creation itself will be set free from decay and share the freedom of the glory of God’s children.

Set free. Not destroyed but renewed (Revelation 21:1–5).

Where Christians differ. Some expect the earth to be annihilated and believers to live in a purely spiritual heaven. This verse expects renewal. Verdict: new heavens and a new earth, this creation restored and glorified.

On a Tuesday. Caring for creation is fitting for those who expect its renewal.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Creation groans like a woman in labour, and so do believers, longing for the redemption of their bodies.

Groaning together. Pain with the promise of birth.

Firstfruits of the Spirit. The Spirit is the first part of the harvest, the pledge of the rest.

Adoption, the redemption of our bodies. Our adoption is complete when our bodies are raised.
verseByVerse.note: The firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, given to God as a pledge of the whole harvest to come.

verseByVerse.quote: For in this hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We were saved in hope, and hope by definition waits for what is not yet seen, with patience.

In this hope. Salvation has a future tense.

Patience. Endurance.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When we do not know how to pray, the Spirit helps our weakness and intercedes for us with groans, according to God’s will.

Groanings too deep for words. Where Christians differ. Some see speaking in tongues here. Most see the Spirit’s own intercession, unspoken. Verdict: the Spirit’s intercession, which God the Father understands perfectly.

According to the will of God. The Spirit’s prayers are always answered.

For worship. When you cannot pray, you are still prayed for.

parallels.desc: you have searched me and known me

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. — Romans 8:28
verseByVerse.commentary:
For those who love God and are called according to his purpose, God works all things together for good.

We know. A certainty, not a slogan.

All things. Including suffering, sin’s consequences and loss.

For good. The good of verse 29: conformity to Christ.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts read “God works all things together for good”. Verdict: either way, God is the one at work.

What it does not mean. Not that all things are good, nor that we will always see the good in this life.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God works all things together for good.”

parallels.desc: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good

verseByVerse.quote: For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son... And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified. — Romans 8:29–30
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s purpose stretches from eternity to eternity: those he foreknew he predestined, called, justified and glorified, to make them like his Son.

Foreknew. Where Christians differ. Arminians read it as God foreseeing who would believe. Reformed theology reads it as God setting his love on people beforehand, as “know” often means in Scripture (Amos 3:2; Jeremiah 1:5). Verdict: foreknowledge here is God’s prior, personal love, not merely foresight.

The golden chain. Each link holds: none foreknown is lost before glorification.

Glorified. Past tense: so certain it is as good as done.

Firstborn among many brothers. The goal is a family like Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “Foreknew” means more than knowing ahead of time: God set his love on them beforehand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–39 — Nothing Can Separate Us from the Love of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter ends with a doxology of certainty — a sustained rhetorical climax in which Paul asks a rapid series of questions, answers each in triumph, and then piles up a list of everything in the universe that might be imagined to separate the Christian from the love of God — only to declare that none of it can. This is not wishful thinking; it is the logical conclusion of everything Paul has argued since 1:16. The gospel that justifies the ungodly will not ultimately abandon the justified; the God who did not spare his own Son will certainly spare those for whom his Son died.

"If God is for us, who can be against us?" (v. 31). The answer is not that no one will be against us — Paul has just described tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, and sword (v. 35). The enemies are real. But no enemy, however powerful, can ultimately prevail against those for whom God himself has declared himself as advocate and champion. The "who" of the question is not answered with "no one" but with "it doesn't matter" — because God's being for us outweighs any opposition.

The concluding list — death, life, angels, rulers, things present, things to come, powers, height, depth, anything else in all creation — is Paul's way of saying: I have tried to think of everything, and I cannot think of anything that can separate you from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. The love of God is not a feeling that fluctuates with our spiritual temperature; it is the settled, sovereign, covenant commitment of the God who gave his Son for us. That love will not let us go — because it has never been dependent on us to begin with.

Two of the questions in between deserve naming, because they are the ones a troubled conscience actually asks. Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? and Who is to condemn? (vv. 33–34). Paul does not answer by denying that there is anything to charge — the first three chapters of this letter were the charge sheet. He answers by naming who occupies the two seats that matter: it is God who justifies, and the one who might condemn is the one who died, was raised, is at the right hand, and is at this moment interceding. The prosecution may say what it likes; the bench and the counsel for the defence are already taken. And then v. 37, which is not a claim that the hardships are avoided: in all these things — the tribulation, the famine, the sword — we are more than conquerors, which means the victory is won inside the trouble rather than by escaping it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Perseverance of the Saints

Romans 8:31–39 is the biblical anchor of the Reformed doctrine of the perseverance (or preservation) of the saints. The saints do not persevere because they are strong; they persevere because God keeps them. The question is not whether we can hold on to God but whether God will hold on to us — and Paul's answer is thunderous. The God who predestined, called, and justified will glorify. Nothing in the universe — not even our own faithlessness — can sever the love that chose us before we existed and purchased us at the cost of the Son. Perseverance is not a human achievement; it is a divine gift, the last link in the golden chain.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's list of hardships in v. 35 — tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, sword — was not hypothetical for his original readers. The Roman church would face Nero's persecution within a decade. Some of them would be burned as torches in Nero's gardens; some would be torn by dogs. Paul writes these verses for people who will need them when the persecution comes. Now: The Christian in the comfortable West reads Romans 8:35–39 as comfort for ordinary difficulties. The Christian in the persecuted church reads it as the word they need to die well. Both readings are valid, and the comfortable Christian is unwise to forget that what sustained the martyrs is the same grace that sustains her — and the same grace may yet be tested in ways she has not anticipated.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God is for us, no one can be against us: the God who gave his Son will give us everything we need.

Who can be against us? Many oppose, but none can prevail.

Did not spare his own Son. An echo of Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 22:12, 16).

All things. If he gave the greatest gift, he will not withhold lesser ones.

parallels.desc: the LORD is on my side; I will not fear
you have not withheld your son

No accusation can stand against God’s chosen, because God justifies them and Christ died, rose and intercedes for them.

Who shall bring a charge? Satan accuses (Revelation 12:10), conscience accuses; the Judge has already acquitted.

Christ intercedes. His presence at the Father’s right hand is a constant plea for us (Hebrews 7:25).

verseByVerse.commentary:
No suffering or danger can separate us from Christ’s love, though Scripture says we will face them.

The list. Paul had experienced most of them (2 Corinthians 11:23–27).

Psalm 44:22. Suffering for God’s sake is part of the life of his people.

In all these things we are more than conquerors through Christ who loved us.

In all these things. Not by escaping them.

More than conquerors. Super-conquerors: suffering itself serves our good.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 8:38–39
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing in all creation can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

I am sure. Persuaded, convinced.

The list. Death and life, spiritual powers, time, space, and anything else created: nothing.

In Christ Jesus. God’s love is fixed on us in his Son.

For worship. Read verses 31–39 at the end of a hard day, and rest.
verseByVerse.note: Paul names every kind of power, time and place, whether seen or unseen.
