accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience—by word and deed,<sup>19</sup>by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God—so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ;<sup>20</sup>and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else’s foundation,<sup>21</sup>but as it is written, “Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.”<sup>22</sup>This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you.<sup>23</sup>But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you,<sup>24</sup>I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while.<sup>25</sup>At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints.<sup>26</sup>For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem.<sup>27</sup>For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.<sup>28</sup>When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you.<sup>29</sup>I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.<sup>30</sup>I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf,<sup>31</sup>that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,<sup>32</sup>so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company.<sup>33</sup>May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

16.title: Greetings, Warnings, and the Final Doxology
16.overview:
Romans 16 is sometimes treated as an appendix — a list of greetings to be skimmed before putting the letter down. It is far more than that. The twenty-six people Paul greets in vv. 3–15 (twenty-four of them by name), with several households besides, constitute a remarkable social portrait of the early Roman church: women who worked hard in the Lord, co-workers who risked their necks for Paul, households that may have belonged to powerful men, and many names common among slaves and freedmen. The community Paul is writing to and for is not an abstraction; it is these people, in this city, with these names and these stories.

The chapter also contains a sharp warning against those who create division and cause obstacles contrary to the doctrine (vv. 17–20) — a reminder that the unity and the gospel Paul has laboured to establish require vigilance as well as love. And then the letter ends where it began: with the gospel. The doxology of vv. 25–27 is one of the most comprehensive summaries of Paul's gospel in the New Testament — the mystery kept secret for long ages, now disclosed through the prophetic Scriptures, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith, to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — A Network of Saints: The Social World of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The list of greetings in Romans 16 is the most extensive in Paul's letters and has rightly been treated as a window into the earliest church. Twenty-six individuals are greeted, twenty-four of them by name, along with several households and groups. The social diversity is remarkable: Phoebe, a deacon and patron from Cenchreae; Priscilla and Aquila, tentmakers and theological teachers; Andronicus and Junia, "well known to the apostles" and Christians before Paul; Epaenetus, the first convert in Asia; Mary, who worked very hard. Slaves and free, women and men, Jews and Gentiles — all members of the same body.

Phoebe (vv. 1–2) deserves special notice: Paul commends her as a deacon (diakonos — the same word used of male church officers) of the church in Cenchreae, and as a patron (prostatis) who has been of help to many, including Paul himself. She was almost certainly the letter-carrier — the person who bore the manuscript of Romans from Corinth to Rome and, as was customary for letter-carriers in antiquity, would have read and explained the letter to its recipients. The greatest theological letter ever written was entrusted to a woman for its first public delivery.

The greeting "holy kiss" (v. 16) — appearing in four of Paul's letters — was the physical expression of the family bond that the gospel created. In the ancient world, the kiss of greeting belonged chiefly to family. The church that greeted one another with a holy kiss was declaring, physically and publicly, that these people — strangers by blood, foreigners by origin, divided by every social category — were family. The gospel had done what nothing else could do: created a new human community that crossed every boundary the ancient world had erected.

Between the famous names and the holy kiss lies the bulk of the list, and it is worth not skipping. Verses 8–15 greet Ampliatus, Urbanus, Stachys, Apelles, the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus, Herodion, Tryphaena and Tryphosa, Persis, Rufus and his mother, then Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas.

Several of those are ordinary slave names, and three of them — Ampliatus, Stachys and Persis — Paul calls beloved. Two are greeted not as individuals but as households — and in one of them only those in the Lord. Three of the workers named in this stretch are women, and one man is remembered chiefly through his mother, who Paul says has been a mother to him as well (v. 13).

And the last two clusters are given no description at all — nine names and an unnamed sister, with nothing attached, followed by the brothers who are with them and all the saints who are with them, who are not named at all. That proportion is the honest shape of the church in every century: a few remembered for something, most remembered only for being there, and the majority not written down.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Humanity

Romans 16:1–16 is the embodiment in flesh-and-blood names of Paul's theological argument in chapters 1–15. The "no distinction between Jew and Greek" of 10:12, the olive tree of Jew and Gentile grafted together of 11:17–24, the "welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you" of 15:7 — all of these are visible in the list of names. This is what the gospel looks like when it has done its work: Phoebe and Priscilla and Andronicus and Junia, the patron and the tentmaker, the first convert and the former persecutor's associates, all belonging to each other in Christ. The doctrine of justification by faith produces a sociology.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The social mixing of Romans 16 was, by the standards of the first-century world, radical to the point of scandalous. Social boundaries in Rome were enforced with rigour; meals with social inferiors were a form of self-humiliation. The church that gathered Phoebe the patron and the slaves of great households and the Jewish tentmakers for common worship and common greeting was an institution the Roman world had no category for. Now: The contemporary church's ability or inability to embody the social diversity of Romans 16 is one of the most important tests of its gospel fidelity. A church that is racially, socially, or economically homogeneous by design has stopped short of what the gospel creates. The greetings of Romans 16 are not an antiquarian curiosity; they are the template for the new humanity the gospel is building.

verseByVerse.quote: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. — Romans 16:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul commends Phoebe, “a servant of the church at Cenchreae,” and asks the Romans to welcome her “in a way worthy of the saints” and help her in whatever she needs, for she has been “a patron of many and of myself as well.” She very probably carried this letter to Rome.

Someone had to carry it. There was no post for private letters; a document travelled because a person carried it. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern harbour, and Romans went from there to Rome in Phoebe’s luggage. The bearer of a letter commonly read it aloud and answered questions about it — the sender’s voice in the room. Romans takes over an hour to read aloud. When the Roman congregations first heard about the potter and the clay, the olive tree, and nothing separating them from God’s love, they most probably heard it in Phoebe’s voice, and when someone asked what Paul meant, she answered.

Two titles. First, diakonos — “servant,” attached here to a particular congregation, “of the church at Cenchreae,” which points to a recognised role rather than a general description. Second, prostatis, “patron” — its only New Testament appearance. In Roman society a patron supplied money, housing, protection and standing to those beneath him. The apostle to the Gentiles is on record as having been somebody’s dependent.

Was Phoebe a deacon in the sense of an office? Some take the word in its general sense: a servant of the church, as every faithful believer is. Others take her to be a deaconess, one of a recognised order of women who served other women, as later churches had. Others again see her as a deacon in the same office as the men of 1 Timothy 3:8–13, and read 1 Timothy 3:11 as speaking of women deacons rather than deacons’ wives. Because Paul ties her to the church at Cenchreae, the more likely reading is that she held a recognised serving role, and churches that appoint women to serve as deacons have good warrant. But the deacon’s office is one of service, not of teaching and ruling; that belongs to the elders (1 Tim 3:2; 5:17), and Phoebe’s honour here does not make her one.

What the text settles. It does not describe her duties. It does establish, as plain fact, that a woman held a recognised position in her congregation, funded the apostle, and was entrusted with delivering and first reading the most important letter he wrote.

Welcome worthy of the saints. Phoebe was arriving in a city where she might know no one. The Romans are told to treat her as one of their own — which in Christ she is — and to help her “in whatever she may need.” That is the early church’s hospitality made concrete.

A test. Who has served you in Christ without much notice — given money, a home, protection, time, or simply carried the message to you? Thank them this week, specifically. And who is newly arrived in your church, knowing no one? Welcome them “in a way worthy of the saints”: ask what they need, and help.
verseByVerse.note: Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. The ESV notes that “servant” can also be rendered “deaconess.” Phoebe probably carried this letter to Rome. A patron was a benefactor who supported others with her resources.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prisca (Priscilla) and Aquila — the tent-making couple who had sheltered Paul in Corinth (Acts 18) and taught Apollos more accurately (Acts 18:26) — are at the top of the list. Risked their necks is almost certainly literal: at some point they placed themselves in mortal danger to protect Paul’s life. The gratitude of all the Gentile churches is owed to them — their courage at a particular moment may have preserved the ministry that evangelized the Gentile world. The personal names in Romans 16 are a reminder that the gospel moves through specific, costly, named human lives.

How does Priscilla’s teaching of Apollos fit with Paul’s I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man (1 Tim 2:12)? Egalitarian Christians see her as proof that Paul placed no such limit on women. But look at what Luke says she did. With her husband she took Apollos aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:26). That was private instruction by a couple, not the authoritative teaching of the gathered church that 1 Timothy 2 reserves for qualified men. The complementarian reading honours both texts. Women may and should teach the faith, to other women (Titus 2:3–5), to children (2 Tim 1:5; 3:15), and in private conversation like this with men too; the office of elder and the preaching of the church belong to men. Paul’s greeting shows how highly he valued her.

Two details in the greeting repay attention. The first is the order of the names. Paul writes Prisca and Aquila, the wife before the husband, and he does so in most of the places where the couple appears. In a world that ordered such things carefully, that is not an accident, and the usual explanation is the simplest one: she was the more prominent of the two, whether by social standing or by gift.

The second is where they are standing when this greeting arrives. They are in Rome — and Paul met them in Corinth because they had been thrown out of Rome, when Claudius expelled the Jews from the city (Acts 18:2). They rebuilt in Corinth, moved on to Ephesus, and have now gone back to the city that had once evicted them. The seam that runs through this whole congregation, and which stands behind so much of chapters 9 to 11 and 14, runs straight through this one household.

And the phrase about their necks is more literal than it sounds: they laid down their own neck for his life — the posture of a man on an executioner’s block. Whatever happened, they put their heads where his was going to be. Paul does not tell us the incident, which suggests everyone concerned already knew it.
verseByVerse.note: Prisca is a form of Priscilla. She and Aquila had returned to Rome after Claudius’s expulsion of Jews ended.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church in their house — the early church met in homes; there were no purpose-built church buildings for centuries. Prisca and Aquila’s home was the gathering place for one of Rome’s house churches, as it had been in Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:19). Epaenetus, the first convert to Christ in Asia — the firstfruits of Paul’s Ephesian ministry, now living in Rome. His presence there is a reminder that the gospel traveled through the empire by moving people, not just ideas: converted in Ephesus, now carrying the faith to Rome.

The word rendered first convert is aparchē, firstfruits — a sacrificial term, the first of the harvest brought to God as the pledge that the rest is coming. Paul has used it already in this letter of the patriarchs (11:16) and of the Spirit we have been given as the down payment on our redemption (8:23). Here he attaches it to one man.

Which fits what he said about his ministry only a chapter ago: that his work is priestly service, and the offering he brings is the Gentiles themselves (15:16). Epaenetus is the first handful of that harvest. Somebody in every place has to be the first, and being first is a lonely business — the first believer in a province has no church to join, no one who understands, and nobody who has done it before him.

It is also worth noticing that a whole congregation is meeting in someone’s front room. No building, no sign, no address anybody would recognise — a house with more people in it than usual on a particular evening. For the first two hundred years or so, that is what the church looked like everywhere.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes; there were no church buildings.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary worked hard — the verb (kopiaō) is the same word Paul uses for his own apostolic labor. Junia is greeted with Andronicus as notable in the apostolic circle, both described as Paul’s kinsmen (fellow Jews) and fellow prisoners — they had shared imprisonment with him, a bond forged in suffering. In Christ before me — they were converts before Paul’s Damascus road encounter, probably part of the earliest Jerusalem community.

Junia raises two questions. The first is whether the name is a man’s or a woman’s. The Greek Iounian can be read as Iounia (feminine — Junia, a common Roman woman’s name) or Iounias (a masculine contraction of Junianus). Chrysostom, in the fourth century, took it as female without hesitation and marvelled that a woman should be counted worthy of the name apostle. Virtually all the early readers understood it the same way, and the masculine Junias has no known attestation in any ancient inscription or literary source. Modern scholarship is near-unanimous that Junia is correct.

The second question is what the phrase about the apostles means. The ESV renders it well known to the apostles — held in high regard by them rather than counted among them — and that is a defensible reading of the Greek; many other translations take it as eminent among the apostles. If the second is right and she is an apostle, she is one in the broader, non-technical sense — a missionary and church-planter, as Barnabas is called an apostle in Acts 14:14 — not in the narrow sense of the Twelve and Paul.

Reformed complementarians generally accept that Junia was a woman, and are divided on whether she was counted in that wider apostolic circle or simply esteemed by it. Nothing here overturns what Paul says elsewhere about the teaching office; what it does show is a woman who shared Paul’s chains for Christ and was honoured by name for it.

Which reading is more likely? Honest scholars still differ on the grammar. On balance the ESV’s well known to the apostles is a little more likely, but the point that matters does not depend on it. If Junia was an apostle, it was in the broader sense of one sent out by a church as a missionary, as Barnabas was (Acts 14:14), not in the office of the Twelve and Paul, whose foundational work ended with them (Eph 2:20). So the verse neither overturns Paul’s teaching on elders nor reopens the apostolic office.

One further note on Mary, who is easily lost between Prisca and Junia. The verb Paul uses of her — kopiaō — means to labour to the point of exhaustion, and it is the word he uses of his own apostolic work. It appears three times in this chapter, and every time it is attached to women: Mary here, then Tryphaena and Tryphosa, and Persis, both at v. 12.

He does not say what any of them did. He says how hard they did it, and that he noticed, and that he wanted a church on the other side of the Mediterranean to know their names. That is not nothing to a person whose work is invisible by nature and unrecorded by default.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the name may be read Junias (a man’s name). Andronicus and Junia had become believers before Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ampliatus, Urbanus, Stachys — common names in Roman slave households, suggesting that the early Roman church included significant numbers from the lower social strata. My beloved in the Lord is Paul’s warmest personal designation: not merely acquaintances or ministry colleagues but those for whom he holds genuine affection rooted in the common life they share in Christ. The church Paul greets is a community of the beloved, held together not by social class or ethnic origin but by their shared belovedness in the Lord.

Sit with what that means for a moment. Ampliatus is a slave’s name — common, unremarkable, the sort of name that appears in household inventories. In the Roman world such a man had no standing, no legal personality worth the term, and no expectation that anyone of consequence would know he existed.

Paul calls him my beloved in the Lord, and puts him in a letter that has been read aloud in every century since. There is a tomb in one of the Roman catacombs bearing the name Ampliatus, cut in unusually careful lettering for so ordinary a name; whether it is this man cannot be shown, but somebody clearly thought an Ampliatus worth honouring.

Which is the sociology the doctrine produces, and it is the reason this chapter is not an appendix. Paul has spent fifteen chapters arguing that God justifies the ungodly and shows no partiality (2:11). Here is what that looks like when it has finished arguing: an apostle listing a slave among the people he loves, by name, in writing, for the record.
verseByVerse.note: Several of these names were common among slaves and freedmen in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus. Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Approved in Christ (dokimos) — the language of testing and verification. Apelles has been tried and found genuine, his faith tested and proved. The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus (likely prominent Roman households whose members had become believers) are greeted as communities within the larger community: the church existed in pockets within Roman society, gathering across the household lines that organized that society. Herodion, another Jewish kinsman, is singled out for personal mention.

The two households repay a moment’s attention, and the details are suggestive even where they cannot be proved. An Aristobulus, a grandson of Herod the Great, had lived in Rome as a private citizen, and a Narcissus of great wealth was a freedman in the imperial service. When such a man died, his household did not disperse; the slaves passed as property to the emperor while keeping their old master’s name. That would explain why Paul greets those who belong to the family of each man rather than the men themselves.

And notice the qualification attached to the second: those in the Lord who belong to the household of Narcissus. Not all of them. Some. Which is a very exact picture of how the faith actually spread through that city — not by converting a great house but by taking root among its servants, a few at a time, in the quarters below.

Then, greeted in the same breath as the household of a Herod, a man named Herodion. The name means belonging to Herod. If the connection is what it appears to be, a member of the family that killed the Baptist and mocked Christ is being greeted as a kinsman and a brother, a few lines from a slave and a woman who works too hard.
verseByVerse.note: The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus probably included their slaves and freedmen.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three women workers in the Lord: Tryphaena and Tryphosa (whose names mean “dainty” and “delicate” — perhaps twins, perhaps ironic given their hard labor) and Persis, who worked hard in the Lord. Women are prominent among Paul’s named co-workers throughout his letters, a pattern that reflects the genuine inclusion of women in the mission of the early church. Rufus (possibly the son of Simon of Cyrene, Mark 15:21) is chosen in the Lord — a mark of particular divine regard; his mother’s care for Paul is remembered with filial gratitude.

That last clause deserves more than a passing mention, because it is one of the warmest things Paul ever wrote and it is over in a single clause: his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.

Consider the man writing it. Paul had no wife and no household. He had been flogged five times, beaten with rods three times, stoned once and left for dead (Acts 14:19), shipwrecked, hungry, cold and short of clothing (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). And somewhere in all that, a woman in Rome took him in and treated him as her own — fed him, presumably made him rest, possibly told him off.

He never gives her name. He identifies her only as somebody’s mother, and that is evidently how he thinks of her. It is worth saying plainly to anyone who has quietly done that for a Christian worker and assumed it counted for little: the apostle put it in Scripture.

And there is a real possibility about the son. Mark, writing his Gospel most likely for the church in Rome, identifies the man pressed into carrying the cross as Simon of Cyrene... the father of Alexander and Rufus (Mark 15:21) — a detail that only makes sense if his readers knew who those two were. It cannot be demonstrated. But it is entirely possible that the woman who mothered Paul was the wife of the man who carried the cross of Christ, and that her son was sitting in one of these house churches when the letter was read out.
verseByVerse.note: Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene, whom Mark mentions as if known to his readers.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two more clusters of house-church communities, each with their circle of unnamed saints. The names span the social spectrum: some are common slave names (Hermes, Hermas), others appear in Roman aristocratic records. The church in Rome was genuinely cross-social — slave and free, men and women, Jews and Gentiles gathered around the one name. All the saints who are with them reminds us that for every named believer in the New Testament, there were hundreds of unnamed ones whose faithfulness built the church that reached us.

These two verses are different from everything before them, and the difference is the point. Nine names and a nameless sister arrive with nothing attached. No my beloved, no who worked hard, no who risked their necks, no approved in Christ. Just Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, Philologus, Julia, Nereus, his sister, Olympas.

We know nothing else about a single one of them. Nereus has a sister whose name was not thought necessary. And behind both clusters stand the ones who are not named at all — the brothers who are with them, all the saints who are with them — rooms full of people reduced to a phrase.

That is the actual proportion of the Christian church, in the first century and in this one. A handful of people are remembered for something. Rather more are remembered only as having been present. The overwhelming majority are not written down anywhere, and every one of them got up on ordinary mornings and believed and was faithful and died.

Paul wrote the names down anyway. He had no way of knowing that in doing so he was putting Patrobas and Olympas into the permanent Scripture of the church, still being read aloud two thousand years later by people who know nothing about them but their names. Which is a fair picture of what God does with obscurity. The register that matters is being kept somewhere else, and it is not short of space.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holy kiss — practiced across the early church as the physical sign of the family bond that the gospel creates — crosses every social barrier that the ancient world erected. Slave and free, Jew and Gentile, male and female greet one another with the same gesture that family members exchange. All the churches of Christ greet you — Paul bears the solidarity of the entire Gentile mission to the Roman church: they are not alone, not isolated, but part of a community spanning the Mediterranean world, united by the name of Christ.

Must Christians greet each other with a kiss today? The command is repeated (1 Cor 16:20; 1 Pet 5:14), but what it commands is the warmth, not the form. In Paul’s world a kiss was an ordinary family greeting; Paul makes it holy, a greeting between brothers and sisters in Christ. Where a kiss carries that meaning it may still be used; where it does not, a handshake or an embrace obeys the command. What is not optional is greeting one another as family.

The command has a small word in it that does all the work: greet one another. Not greet the people you would naturally greet. In a congregation that has spent two chapters arguing about food and days, and that contains a Herodian, several slaves, a wealthy patroness and an unknown number of people who find each other difficult, one another is a considerably more demanding instruction than it looks.

And the closing line does something quietly generous. All the churches of Christ greet you — congregations in Corinth and Philippi and Ephesus, most of whom have never met a single person on this list, sending their greetings to strangers. Paul is telling a church he has never visited that it is already being thought about by people it will never meet.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — Final Warning and the Doxology of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before the closing doxology, Paul inserts a sharp warning (vv. 17–20) against those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine the Romans have been taught. The letter has been, among other things, a sustained argument for the unity of the body across the strong/weak divide; it would be a bitter irony if the letter itself became a tool of division. Paul's instruction is clear: watch them, avoid them. The divisive person — whatever their theological credentials — is not serving Christ but their own appetites, and they deceive the naive with smooth talk and flattery.

The closing doxology (vv. 25–27) returns to the letter's great themes for one final, comprehensive statement. God is able to strengthen — the power of the gospel is not an argument but a strengthening. According to Paul's gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ — these are identified: Paul's gospel is the gospel of Jesus Christ, not a human theological construct. According to the revelation of the mystery kept secret for long ages — the gospel is not a new invention; it is the disclosure of what God planned from before time began. Now made known to all the nations — the universality Paul has argued throughout. For the obedience of faith — the phrase that bracketed the letter in 1:5 now closes it. To the only wise God — the doxology of chapter 11 returns, now applied to the whole letter's argument. Through Jesus Christ — the mediator of all grace and all glory. To whom be glory forever. Amen.

The letter that began with Paul introducing himself as a slave of Christ and set apart for the gospel ends with everything returning to God — from him, through him, and to him. The argument is complete. The doxology is the only adequate conclusion. Amen.

Two stretches sit between the warning and the doxology and should not be passed over. The first is v. 19, where Paul softens nothing but changes his tone: their obedience is known everywhere and he is glad of them, and what he wants is that they be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. It is the counterpart to the warning — the way to be undeceived is not to become worldly-wise about corruption but to know goodness well.

The second is vv. 21–24, a second greeting list, this time from Paul’s end of the journey: Timothy and three Jewish co-workers; Gaius, in whose house both Paul and the whole Corinthian church are lodged; Erastus, the city treasurer, whose name has plausibly been found on a paving inscription at Corinth; and Quartus. Between them stands v. 22, where Tertius, who wrote this letter, adds a greeting of his own — the only place in the New Testament where the man holding the pen speaks in his own voice.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery Revealed: Gospel and Old Testament Unity

Romans 16:25–27 returns to the theme announced in 1:1–4: the gospel was promised beforehand through the prophets; the Old Testament is the gospel in anticipation; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment. The "mystery" kept secret for long ages is not something the Old Testament was ignorant of but something it was pregnant with — the inclusion of the Gentiles in the covenant people, the extension of the Abrahamic blessing to all nations, the righteousness of God given through faith in Jesus Christ. Calvin's canon of interpretation applies: the two testaments are one Bible, one gospel, one covenant of grace, administered differently but pointing to the same Saviour.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The warning of vv. 17–20 against divisive teachers was written into the most doctrinally comprehensive letter Paul ever wrote. The letter's very depth makes it susceptible to misuse: its teachings on election, freedom, and grace can all be distorted into weapons of division. Paul's warning is therefore structurally appropriate — the deeper the theology, the greater the need for vigilance against those who weaponise it. Now: Every generation produces its version of the smooth-talking divisive teacher who uses theological language to advance personal agendas and create factions. Paul's three-fold response is the standing instruction: watch them carefully; avoid them; trust the God of peace who will soon crush Satan under your feet (v. 20).

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. — Romans 16:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
The command is pointed and practical: watch and avoid. The divisive teacher is not to be engaged endlessly in debate or accommodated indefinitely in the hope that he will improve. He is to be identified and avoided — not with contempt, but with the clear-sightedness of people who know what they have been taught and can recognise a deviation when they see it.

contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught — the standard of judgment is not novelty versus tradition, or majority versus minority opinion. It is the apostolic teaching — the gospel Paul has spent sixteen chapters expounding. The community that has this letter has the measuring rod. Apply it. And where teaching measures short or crooked, act accordingly.

Verse 18 then tells you how to recognise them, and the marks are not doctrinal so much as personal. Such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites — literally their own belly, the organ of appetite. Whatever is being said at the front, something is being fed at the back: money, or a following, or the pleasure of being the one who sees what others have missed.

And the method named is not argument. It is smooth talk and flattery. The divisive man in Paul’s description does not begin by attacking the church; he begins by being remarkably nice to you. He tells you that you are more discerning than the others, that you have noticed what they have not. Flattery is the tool because it recruits — you cannot build a faction out of people you have insulted.

His targets are named too: the hearts of the naive, the innocent, those without guile. Not fools. Good-hearted people who assume others mean what they say, which is why the very next verse asks for a particular kind of shrewdness — wise about good, innocent of evil.

A guard is essential here, because this verse is one of the most abused in the letter and the abuse is easy. Paul has just spent two chapters commanding these same people not to separate over disputed matters — not to judge, not to despise, to welcome the man whose conscience differs (14:1–15:7). He cannot be undoing that a chapter later. Romans 16:17 is not a licence to avoid the Christian who disagrees with you.

The marks he gives are specific and all three are needed: the teaching is contrary to what they were taught, the man is serving himself, and he works by flattery rather than by open argument. Someone who holds a different view of the disputed thing and says so plainly is the person chapter 14 told you to welcome. Someone who is quietly assembling a party around himself is the person this verse tells you to walk away from. The difference is not how strongly he disagrees. It is what he is building.

verseByVerse.quote: For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil — the positive and negative of the same counsel. In a world of sophisticated evil and manipulation, the Christian is to be genuinely knowledgeable about goodness (not naive) and genuinely innocent of evil (not sophisticated in wickedness). The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet — an echo of Genesis 3:15 (the first gospel promise: the seed of the woman will crush the serpent’s head), now applied to the whole community through their union with Christ who has already won the decisive victory.

Hold the two halves of v. 20 together, because the combination is startling. The God of peace will crush Satan under your feet. The verb is violent — to break in pieces, to grind — and it is attached to the title Paul has just used at the end of the previous chapter for the God he commends to them (15:33).

That is not a contradiction, and the letter has been explaining why for sixteen chapters. Peace is not made by leaving the hostility in place. It is made by dealing with what caused it, which is why this letter opened with wrath and arrived at reconciliation. A God of peace who could not crush anything would have no peace to offer.

And the promise is put in a strange place: under your feet. Not under Christ’s — though Genesis 3:15 said the serpent would bruise the heel of the woman’s seed, and that was settled at the cross. Paul hands the victory out to a mixed, quarrelling congregation of slaves and patrons and former idolaters, and tells them the last act will happen under their shoes.

Then soon, which has to be faced honestly rather than hurried past. It has been two thousand years. The New Testament consistently speaks this way, and the honest reading is not that Paul miscalculated but that he is describing a decisive outcome that is fixed and imminent in the only sense that matters — the next thing on the agenda, whatever the interval turns out to be.

Which is a word for the reader who is tired of waiting, and who has been waiting in this letter since 8:23. The groaning is real, and Paul never suggests otherwise. But the sentence is not may God crush. It is will. What is left is not the outcome but the interval.
verseByVerse.note: The promise echoes God’s word to the serpent in Eden.

parallels.desc: he shall bruise your head

verseByVerse.quote: Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy, Paul’s closest colleague throughout the Gentile mission, sends greetings — a sign of the collegial nature of Paul’s apostolic work. The three Jewish co-workers (his kinsmen) represent the Jewish component of what has been a predominantly Gentile mission. And then Tertius breaks through: the amanuensis who wrote the letter inserts his own greeting. He is not merely a scribe — he is a brother in Christ, himself a member of the church sending the letter, a co-laborer in the work of preserving and transmitting Paul’s apostolic word.

Stop on this, because it is the only moment of its kind in the New Testament. For hours — more likely days, across several sittings — a man has been sitting with a pen, taking down the words of Romans as Paul spoke them. He has written the wrath of chapter 1 and the no-condemnation of chapter 8. He has written out the potter and the clay. He has just taken down a list of more than twenty names.

And at the end he is either invited to add a line or asks whether he may, and he writes: I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord. The pen looks up.

His name is worth noticing too. Tertius means Third. A verse later a brother called Quartus sends his greeting, and Quartus means Fourth. Numeral names like these were common among slaves and freedmen — the sort sometimes given by owners who did not trouble to think of a name and simply counted.

So the last stretch of the greatest letter ever written contains two men called Three and Four, one of whom physically wrote it. Neither, perhaps, was given a name anyone had troubled over. Both have been read aloud in every language on earth for two thousand years.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters; Tertius was the scribe who wrote this one down.

verseByVerse.quote: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gaius (likely the Corinthian Gaius of 1 Corinthians 1:14, baptized by Paul) hosted Paul and hosted the whole church — a man of sufficient means and sufficient generosity to open his home as the gathering place for the entire Corinthian community. Erastus the city treasurer (oikonomos) is remarkable: an inscription found at Corinth, which may well name him, reads “Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid the pavement at his own expense.” A senior municipal official belonging to the Corinthian church — evidence that the gospel had penetrated even the highest levels of Corinthian civic life.

Set the three men in this verse beside each other and the whole argument of the letter is standing in one room. Erastus holds municipal office, and an inscription that may be his records a street paved at his own expense. Quartus is called Fourth, a name common among slaves. Gaius is generous enough to be host to Paul and to the whole church.

They are sending a joint greeting. The city treasurer and the man named after a number are in the same sentence, on the same footing, and the only title Quartus needs is brother. In Corinth, outside that house, they may have had no relationship the law could have described.

That is what Paul meant back at 2:11 when he said God shows no partiality, and at 10:12 when he said there is no distinction. He did not mean it as a sentiment. He meant that a room would eventually exist in which it was simply true, and he is writing from one.
verseByVerse.note: An inscription found at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a street at his own expense, perhaps the same man.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second benediction of grace — the word that opened the letter (1:5, 1:7) closes it. From first to last, Romans is a letter about grace: the grace of apostleship (1:5), the grace of justification (3:24), the grace of election (11:5), the grace of spiritual gifts (12:6), and now the closing grace of the Lord Jesus Christ commended to the whole community. Nothing is more fitting as the final word of the greatest letter ever written about the gospel than the name and grace of the one the gospel is about.

One textual note, briefly, because readers comparing translations will notice it. Verse 24 is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts, and most modern versions either omit it or print it in a footnote — it appears to be a copyist’s repetition of the benediction already given at the end of v. 20. If your Bible skips from v. 23 to v. 25, that is why, and nothing whatever is lost: the sentence is genuinely Paul’s, it is simply Paul’s from four verses earlier.

It is worth saying that this is what a well-attested text looks like rather than a problem with it. The variant is visible, small, and doctrinally weightless — a scribe reaching for a familiar ending, and the manuscript evidence sufficient to show exactly what he did.

And the instinct behind the addition was sound, whoever had it. Grace is how this letter starts (1:7) and grace is how it should stop. A copyist who felt that the argument could not simply end had understood something about the book he was copying.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 24: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith —
verseByVerse.commentary:
The doxology that closes Romans is addressed to God who is able to strengthen you — and the means of that strengthening is my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ. The gospel is not merely information about Christ; it is the power by which God strengthens his people (cf. 1:16). The mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed is the inclusion of the Gentiles in the one people of God through the Messiah — the great open secret that the prophets pointed toward and that Paul has been expounding throughout the letter. The command of the eternal God drives the Gentile mission.

The opening verb closes a loop opened in the first chapter. Paul told them at 1:11 that he longed to come and give them some spiritual gift to strengthen them. He never managed it — hindered, then hindered again, and when he finally arrived it was in chains. So the letter ends by handing the task over: to him who is able to strengthen you. What the apostle wanted to do and could not, God can do without him.

Then the phrase that closes the largest loop of all. The gospel has been made known to all nations, says v. 26, to bring about the obedience of faith — which is word for word what Paul said his apostleship was for in the fifth verse of the letter (1:5). The first paragraph and the last paragraph of Romans say the same thing. Everything between is the argument for it.

Does the obedience of faith make obedience part of what saves us? No. Paul means the obedience that faith is and the obedience faith produces: to believe the gospel is to obey God’s summons, and those who believe go on to obey. It is the same phrase as in 1:5, and the whole letter between those two verses has argued that we are justified by faith apart from works (3:28). Obedience is the fruit of faith, never its price.

And there is a deliberate paradox in the middle worth pausing on: a mystery kept secret for long ages which has nonetheless been made known through the prophetic writings. Secret, and in writing the whole time.

Which is exactly right, and anyone who has read chapters 9 to 11 has watched it demonstrated. Hosea and Isaiah and Moses and the Psalms were saying that the nations would come in. It was on the page in every synagogue. What was missing was not the information but the event that makes the information legible — and once Christ had come, Paul could go back through the same scrolls and show that they had been saying it all along. A mystery in Paul’s sense is not a puzzle nobody could solve. It is something that could not be seen until God did the thing it was about.

Kept secret for long ages, and now disclosed. All that time — the promise to Abraham, the exodus, the law, the kings, the exile, the silence — God was holding something back that he fully intended to say. Nothing was being improvised. The nations were in the plan before there was a nation, and the ungodly were in it before there was anyone who was not.

Every page of the Old Testament was written by someone who did not know how the sentence ended, and was carried by someone who did.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The only wise God — not one wise being among many, but the only one whose wisdom is absolute, uncreated, inexhaustible, and without rival. All of Romans has been a display of divine wisdom: the wisdom that designed salvation through the cross, that included the Gentiles through Israel’s stumbling, that will bring Israel in through the Gentiles’ fullness. Be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ — all glory returns to God through the mediation of the Son, who is both the agent of creation and the mediator of new creation. Amen: so it is, and so it shall be, world without end.

It is worth admitting what the sentence does grammatically, because it is a small window into the man. Read vv. 25–27 as one sentence and it does not parse. It begins now to him who is able to strengthen you, accumulates clause after clause — according to my gospel, according to the revelation, kept secret, now disclosed, through the prophetic writings, according to the command — and then never returns to complete the thought, arriving instead at to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ. The relative pronoun at the end has no clear home.

Commentators have worried at it for centuries. The plainest explanation is the human one. He set out to say something about God and could not get to the end of the subject, and the sentence simply gives way under the weight and turns into worship. The last sentence of Romans is broken because Paul could not finish it.

He has done this once before, at the end of chapter 11, when the argument about Israel ran out into oh, the depth of the riches. Both times the same thing happens: the reasoning goes as far as reasoning goes, and then the only available next move is glory. That is not the failure of the theology. It is what the theology is for.

And so the letter stops. It began with a man calling himself a slave, set apart for a gospel promised beforehand through the prophets, sent to bring about the obedience of faith among all the nations (1:1–5). Sixteen chapters later, having been through wrath and justification and baptism and the wretched man and no condemnation and the potter and the olive tree and the living sacrifice and the weak brother and the greetings from Three and Four, it ends on the same three things: the gospel, the nations, and the obedience of faith. Nothing has been added to the first paragraph. It has been opened.

The last word given to the Roman church is not an instruction, and it is not a summary. Paul has argued them out of every ground of confidence they had and left them with a God who justifies the ungodly. There is only one thing to do with a God like that, and it is the thing this letter has been driving at from the first verse: to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ. Amen.

To the only wise God. In the end there is no one else to give it to. Not the reader, who contributed nothing; not the apostle, who said so himself; not the church, which exists because of it; not the law, which could only measure the damage. One God, wise where nobody else could see, glorified forever, through Jesus Christ.

The letter that began with a man calling himself a slave ends with the whole of creation going home to God, and the last word is not an argument. It is Amen.
